items.title: Η Kelly Clarkson τραγούδησε μια απαίσια εκδοχή του "Stayin' Alive" των Bee Gees για το Halloween
items.titleOriginal: Kelly Clarkson sang a ghoulish version of the Bee Gees’ ‘Stayin’ Alive’ for Halloween
items.description: Το “Stayin’ Alive” των Bee Gees είναι ένα υπέροχο τραγούδι για πολλούς λόγους. Έχει να κάνει με την επιβίωση στη μεγάλη πόλη, και το προωστικό τυμπανάκι της ντίσκο είναι τόσο κοντά σε έναν τυπικό καρδιακό παλμό που οι εκπαιδευτές CPR ζητούν από τους ανθρώπους να το βουίζουν στο κεφάλι τους ενώ κάνουν θωρακικές συμπιέσεις. Φαίνεται ότι το 1977, με το τραγούδι, οι Bee Gees έφτασαν στον πυρήνα του τι είναι εγώ…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Stayin’ Alive” by the Bee Gees is a great song for many reasons. It’s about survival in the big city, and its propulsive disco drumbeat is so close to a typical heartbeat that CPR instructors ask people to hum it in their heads while administering chest compressions . It seems that in 1977, with the song, the Bee Gees got to the core of what it means to be human and did so in amazing white silk pants. “[“Stayin’ Alive”] was based on Tony having a big night out in New York and the whole concept of being famous by dancing,” the Bee Gees’ Barry Gibb said, according to uDiscoverMusic . “The title came up real early on, but then the song started to evolve. The title is really what the song means about surviving on the streets, sort of a social comment.” Kelly Clarkson sings ‘Stayin’ Alive’ Talk show host Kelly Clarkson took the song’s meaning a step further by singing it in the Halloween edition of her Kellyoke segment. Clarkson sang it against a backdrop of bodies rising from the grave, turning the song’s meaning into an impassioned fight for her life. For this version, instead of surviving on the streets of New York City in the late ‘70s, Clarkson had to sing her way through a night of terror. For the performance, Clarkson dressed as Madeline Ashton, Meryl Streep’s character from 1992’s Death Becomes Her . At the beginning of the performance, she’s joined by background singers: one dressed as Goldie Hawn’s character and another as Ernest, who was played by Bruce Willis. “Look at this mansion, though! This is amazing, y’all. It’s just like the one Meryl lived in,” Clarkson said . “Those are actually the stairs Ernest pushed her down. There are the candelabras and, of course, Meryl’s portrait, which I’m seriously considering just keeping up year-round because I love her.” What’s interesting is that after a slowed-down intro, the song picks up the pace and gets an ‘80s Michael Jackson “Thriller” vibe, which lets Clarkson show off her powerful voice. Her take contrasts sharply with the falsetto sung by Barry Gibb and his brothers in the original version. Clarkson has never been quiet about her love for Meryl Streep To Clarkson fans, it’s not a huge surprise that she dressed up as a character from a Meryl Streep film; the talk show host hasn’t been quiet about her love for her. When Clarkson met Streep in 2018 at the Golden Globes, she told the Mamma Mia! star that she had been a huge fan of her since she was 8. In 2019, Clarkson launched an online campaign, #FromKellyToMeryl, to try to get Streep to appear on her show. Sadly, for Clarkson, it still hasn’t happened. Last year, Clarkson sang ‘I Put a Spell on You’ for Halloween In 2025, Clarkson dressed as Bette Midler from Hocus Pocus and gave a scorching performance of “I Put a Spell on You, originally popularized by Screamin’ Jay Hawkins. The post Kelly Clarkson sang a ghoulish version of the Bee Gees’ ‘Stayin’ Alive’ for Halloween appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το κλιπ του Rowan Atkinson που «γίνεται» στον Mr. Bean δείχνει πώς η υποκριτική μπορεί να είναι τόσο απλή όσο το να γουρλώνεις τα μάτια σου
items.titleOriginal: Clip of Rowan Atkinson ‘becoming’ Mr. Bean illustrates how acting can be as simple as rolling your eyes
items.description: Ο αγαπημένος χαρακτήρας Mr. Bean υπήρχε χρόνια πριν ο ηθοποιός Rowan Atkinson τον ονομάσει, και ο Atkinson μπορεί να μην το είχε καν συνειδητοποιήσει. Ως άνθρωπος με πολλά πρόσωπα, η ικανότητά του να φέρνει χαρακτήρες στον κόσμο έξω από τον αιθέρα είναι εκπληκτική. Μέχρι το 1981, ο Άτκινσον ήταν 26 ετών και ήταν ήδη καθιερωμένος κωμικός ηθοποιός, τουλάχιστον στη μία πλευρά της λίμνης. Fo…
items.descriptionOriginal: The beloved character Mr. Bean existed years before actor Rowan Atkinson even named him , and Atkinson may not even have realized it. As a man of many faces, his ability to bring characters into the world out of the ether is astounding. By 1981, Atkinson was 26 years old and already an established comedic actor, at least on one side of the pond. For nearly three years, he had been a sketch performer on the show Not the Nine O’Clock News . Around that time, he appeared on Sir Michael Parkinson’s talk show , BBC One’s Parkinson . It was then and there that a character was presented to the world. View this post on Instagram ‘Ordinary’ person on a train In a resurfaced clip from the interview posted on Instagram, Atkinson describes a very “ordinary” person on a train. He sits in his suit and tie and explains that with just a simple change of his facial expression, he can transform into an entirely different, hilarious (and peculiar) person. He describes this mysterious human, saying, “The person sitting opposite you on the train behaves like…” He cuts himself off, realizing he’d rather show than tell. “I can demonstrate a very ordinary, very inoffensive person doing nothing, but somehow being funny. He stands up, he’s doing nothing, and he sits down.” Atkinson physically acts out standing and sitting, bending his knees in and hunching over. And just like that, you can see the split second Bean comes to life. He stretches his face, licks his lips, and bulges out his eyes, much to the delight of the studio audience. He further crosses his arms uncomfortably and lets out a giant sigh. He looks at the (invisible) person next to him and smiles, then averts his eyes in an insecure yet charming way. Not a single word It’s a sight to behold. He said absolutely nothing, yet his entire demeanor shifted. About ten years later, Mr. Bean would come to life in his own sitcom, later delighting audiences worldwide with multiple films. The character had only been a wisp of an idea years earlier. Atkinson explains to Outstanding Screenplays that ITV had simply needed a filler. “ITV was looking to fill this one gap in the schedule,” he said. “The screenwriter and I had met when we were both students at Oxford. And we had already done some visual sketches. I had discovered by then, I suppose, that I could express myself without words.” Various outlets have shared the clip, including an Instagram page ( @paidjoke ) best known for pop culture memes and clips. They write, “Man, the moment he transforms into Mr. Bean is absurd. Honestly nothing humbles you quite like realizing your entire personality is just five different variations of sitting quietly while mentally screaming until it is socially acceptable to leave.” ‘True cinema’ The Instagram post alone has received over 1.6 million likes and nearly 5,000 comments in just two days. One person shared that it helped them understand the character’s genius: “I now finally understand Mr. Bean. A man with high emotional and intellectual intelligence can only exist when you truly know anxiety and insecurity. To feel confident is also to feel at home with knowing what self-consciousness really is. And to demonstrate it for film and emphasize it, is true cinema.” Another notes how incredible the transformation was. “It’s like a whole different person stood up and another person sat down.” Another Instagrammer points out how something as small as a sigh or a yawn can create such hilarity. “This person made millions of people laugh without saying anything.” The post Clip of Rowan Atkinson ‘becoming’ Mr. Bean illustrates how acting can be as simple as rolling your eyes appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η Ariana Grande εξέπληξε έναν δρομέα Μαραθωνίου της Νέας Υόρκης με ένα ευγενικό σημείωμα που έγραψε ενώ παρακολουθούσε τον αγώνα
items.titleOriginal: Ariana Grande surprised an NYC Marathon runner with a kind note she wrote while watching the race
items.description: Φέτος, ο Μαραθώνιος της Νέας Υόρκης πραγματοποιήθηκε την Κυριακή 1 Νοεμβρίου. Πάνω από 59.000 δρομείς διέσχισαν τη γραμμή τερματισμού και 200.000 θεατές παρατάχθηκαν στους δρόμους των πέντε συνοικιών της πόλης. Η ποπ σταρ και ηθοποιός Ariana Grande ήταν μια από τις ενθουσιασμένες θεατές που βγήκαν στους δρόμους της Νέας Υόρκης για να επευφημήσουν τους δρομείς. Μαζί με τον φίλο της Ρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: This year, the New York City Marathon took place on Sunday, November 1st. Over 59,000 runners crossed the finish line , and a whopping 200,000 spectators lined the streets of the city’s five boroughs. Pop star and actress Ariana Grande was one of the excited onlookers who took to the streets of NYC to cheer on the runners. Alongside her boyfriend Ricky Alvarez, Grande was spotted in the crowd by content creator Ella Schweiger , creator of Ella’s Envelope. Schweiger was at the NYC Marathon to pass out kind notes to runners, written by spectators in her massive Ella’s Envelope. When Schweiger asked Grande to write one, Grande was all in. View this post on Instagram Ariana Grande at NYC Marathon In a video shared on Instagram, Schweiger captured the moment she approached Grande. Grande was trying to stay incognito, wearing a face mask and sipping an iced coffee alongside Alvarez. “Excuse me, can I ask you a question?” Schweiger says as she approaches Grande. “I am delivering kind messages in this big envelope to runners that are running today. Would you guys write a message?” Grand replies, “Sure! That’s cute!” as she takes a pen and a piece of paper from Schweiger. “Are you sure?” Schweiger responds, as Grande says, “Yeah, why not?” Schweiger thanks her excitedly. Once done writing her message, Grandev hands it over, saying, “There you go! That’s such a great thing!” Schweiger tells Grande, “Thank you so much! I’ll post it in the envelope!” Ecstatic, Schweiger turns to the camera and brandishes Grande’s note. “Ariana Grande has just written a message for my envelope. I’m shaking!” she squeals. She then read what Grande wrote: “You did it!” alongside three hand-drawn hearts. Grande signed it “Ari + Ricky.” View this post on Instagram Grande’s note delivered to NYC Marathon finisher In the next clip, Schweiger puts Grand’s note into her big Ella’s Envelope. She approaches a finisher named Ellie, who is wrapped in an orange post-race blanket, and asks if she’d like a kind note from a stranger. “This is so sweet!” Ellie says as she reaches into the envelope for the note. “It says: ‘You did it! From Ari and Ricky.'” That’s when Schweiger reveals who actually wrote it. “No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no…I can’t believe you picked that one! That’s from Ariana Grande! She wrote that this morning!” says Schweiger. “Are you serious?!” Ellie asks repeatedly, then reveals she was listening to Grande’s hit song “The Way” during Mile 24. “It got me through!” Ellie adds. “So I love me some Ariana Grande. Wait, are you serious?!” Schweiger then asks her what got Ellie through the toughest moments of the race, “besides Ariana Grande.” Ellie shares, “Except for knowing that I would get [a note] of Ariana Grande’s, honestly, it was them [she says as she points to her crew]. Knowing that so many of my friends and family showed up. And the energy…I’ve never experienced anything like that. People saying my name, I don’t know, and people like you, honestly!” The post Ariana Grande surprised an NYC Marathon runner with a kind note she wrote while watching the race appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το σκετς «Delta Disruptive» της SNL μετατρέπει την παραφροσύνη που συμβαίνει στις αεροπορικές εταιρείες της Αμερικής σε χρυσό κωμωδίας
items.titleOriginal: SNL’s ‘Delta Disruptive’ sketch spins the insanity happening on America’s airlines into comedy gold
items.description: Σε έναν κόσμο όπου όλοι έχουν τώρα μια κάμερα, μια σκοτεινή πλευρά της ταξιδιωτικής βιομηχανίας της Αμερικής έχει εκτεθεί. Οι άνθρωποι προκαλούν χάος στις εμπορικές αεροπορικές εταιρείες και φαίνεται ότι ένας νέος απείθαρχος επιβάτης γίνεται viral κάθε εβδομάδα. Πριν από τρία χρόνια, η Tiffany Gomas έγινε διαβόητη αφού ούρλιαξε για ένα άτομο που «δεν είναι αληθινό» σε μια πτήση από το Ντάλας στο Ορλάντο. Th…
items.descriptionOriginal: In a world where everyone now has a camera, a dark side of America’s travel industry has been exposed. People are causing chaos on commercial airlines , and it seems like a new unruly passenger goes viral every week. Three years ago, Tiffany Gomas became infamous after screaming about a person who “isn’t real” on a flight from Dallas to Orlando. There was also Maxwell Berry , the man who got duct-taped to his seat after groping two flight attendants and punching a third on a Frontier Airlines flight. There’s also been an assortment of hair-pullers, drunks, and people who can’t get through a flight without screaming racial slurs . SNL’s ‘Delta Disruptive’ sketch The folks at Saturday Night Live had fun with the shenanigans in the friendly skies, with a pre-recorded sketch in which Ashley Padilla, dressed as Tanya Davis, Delta’s director of in-flight service, announces a new section of the plane for unruly passengers: Delta Disruptive. “At Delta, we try to provide a safe, enjoyable flight to everyone,” Padilla says. “Unfortunately, incidents of unruly behavior are on the rise. Nobody should have to deal with the stress of a disorderly passenger on their flight. And now, they won’t have to, introducing Delta Disruptive, a new section of the plane, exclusively for crazy people.” The sketch features host Inde Navarrete playing a Gomas-style character who sees shadow people on the plane and wears pants that expose a bit too much of her posterior. Cast member Mikey Day plays a man who slams the overhead bins ‘til they break and tries to open the emergency exit. Tommy Brennan proudly reads Mein Kampf by Adolf Hitler in the Disruptive section, and Sarah Sherman gets taped to a chair for attempting to stab someone with a pen. A Delta flight taking off. Photo credit: Thomas Arnoux/Flickr Delta Disruptive is safe, at least for those in the other sections “And if you’re worried that a section full of crazy people won’t be safe, don’t be,” Padilla continues. “All Delta Disruptive flight attendants are the toughest, gayest ex-Spirit Airlines employees who have seen much worse.” Cut to Kennan Thompson trying to take control of the disruptive section by yeeting an emotional support lizard out of the emergency exit. One decent way to track this: FAA data on “unruly passenger reports” shows a much higher level of anti-social behavior relative to pre-COVID baseline. https://t.co/B5eOecgeSC pic.twitter.com/bepG1fAOzy — Alec Stapp (@AlecStapp) December 6, 2024 The sketch raises an important question: are airline passengers getting more disruptive, or has this always been happening and nobody had a camera phone to record it? According to the Federal Aviation Administration , incidents have been rising for nearly a decade. In 2017, there were 544 reports of unruly passengers; in 2021, incidents grew by more than 10 times due to mask mandates, reaching 5,973. In 2026, there have already been over 1,400 reports, but that’s a big drop from the 2021 spike. Why are passengers more unruly these days? According to an NPR report , it stems from several factors. First, planes are more packed than ever, leading to more stress during boarding and less comfort while flying. There’s been an increase in people drinking and mixing with medications, and finally, in a post-pandemic world, people seem to have shorter fuses. Let’s hope that the number of people who lose their minds on flights starts to drop a bit; we don’t want Delta Disruptive to go from a joke to the new section you have to walk through to get to the bathroom. The post SNL’s ‘Delta Disruptive’ sketch spins the insanity happening on America’s airlines into comedy gold appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το Korea Girl ήταν ένα ξεχασμένο συγκρότημα της δεκαετίας του '90 μέχρι που οι Gen Zers βρήκαν το τραγούδι τους και το έπαιξαν 92 εκατομμύρια φορές
items.titleOriginal: Korea Girl was a forgotten ’90s band until Gen Zers found their song and played it 92 million times
items.description: Πολλοί καλλιτέχνες προσυπογράφουν τη φιλοσοφία «τέχνη για την τέχνη». Επινοημένο από τον Γάλλο φιλόσοφο του 19ου αιώνα Victor Cousin, το «l’art pour l’art» σημαίνει ότι η τέχνη δεν χρειάζεται να δικαιολογείται και επικεντρώνεται στην αυτοέκφραση και στην ίδια τη δημιουργική πράξη. Είναι κάτι που η Elizabeth Yi και η indie rock μπάντα της από το San Jose, California, Korea Girl, ακολούθησαν το 199…
items.descriptionOriginal: Many artists subscribe to the philosophy “ art for art’s sake .” Coined by 19th-century French philosopher Victor Cousin, “l’art pour l’art” means that art need not be justified and centers on self-expression and the creative act itself. It’s something Elizabeth Yi and her indie rock band from San Jose, California, Korea Girl , followed back in 1997, when they recorded their song “Reunion.” At the time, the song was far from a “hit.” It sat for nearly 30 years until Gen Z resurrected it through TikTok. Today, it has over 92 million streams on Spotify . View this post on Instagram The start of Korea Girl Korea Girl was formed in 1996. It included members Elizabeth Yi, Tobin Mori, Summer Farnese, and Mark Duarte. They recorded their first songs in March 1996 and released their first album in 1997. The band’s self-titled CD, Korea Girl , wasn’t a total flop. It earned a “Bammie” nomination from the Bay Area Music Awards, founded by BAM magazine in 1977. A high honor, other nominees for a “Bammie” that year included Metallica, Journey, Cake, Chris Isaak & Silvertone, and the Counting Crows. But a second album never came, and the band broke up in 1999 . “Reunion” has a second life Yi wrote “Reunion” in 1996 after she was invited to her 10-year high school reunion at Edmonds-Woodway High School in Edmonds, Washington. It was an invitation she would refuse, and she put her feelings about it to paper. “Liz really wasn’t like an indie rock person; she’s just extremely honest,” bandmate Tobin Mori said of lead singer Yi in an excerpt from the recently released book Elvis is Dead, I’m Still Alive, by author and musician Mike Huguenor , as reported by Metro Silicon Valley . “In a good way. She had a great sensibility. It comes through in her songs.” “Reunion” is described in Elvis is Dead as “jangly and mid-tempo,” and it features Yi’s honest lyrics. In the chorus, she sings, “Why would I spend more time with people that I hate, couldn’t wait to leave behind?” Gen Z recently found the track through TikTok. The audio for “Reunion” began going viral on the social media app in the fall of 2025. It was Yi’s niece, Jamie, who told her aunt the song was “blowing up” there after one of her friends showed it to her. According to the San Francisco Chronicle , the friend apparently had no idea Jamie was related to the lead singer. “I just froze; ‘That’s my aunt’s band’,” Jamie told the newspaper. View this post on Instagram Korea Girl’s story is proof that art never dies. “Elizabeth didn’t spend 30 years trying to make this song go viral. She didn’t have this incredible rollout or marketing plan or label behind her,” producer Kato shared in an Instagram post on the song’s resurgence. “The song didn’t change. The audience did. And I think this is a lesson every single artist and musician needs to understand today.” He adds that today “instant results” mean success—that if something doesn’t “blow up in 30 or 60 days, we feel like it was a complete failure.” But for Korea Girl’s song “Reunion,” there is clearly no expiration date for good music. The post Korea Girl was a forgotten ’90s band until Gen Zers found their song and played it 92 million times appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Γιαπωνέζος μοιράζεται το ημερολόγιο της αδερφής της το 1998 όταν ήταν 16χρονη φοιτήτρια ξένου συναλλάγματος στην Αϊόβα
items.titleOriginal: Japanese man shares sister’s 1998 diary when she was a 16-year-old foreign exchange student in Iowa
items.description: Όταν η Yuki ήταν 16 ετών, ήταν γιαπωνέζα φοιτήτρια ανταλλαγής για περίπου ένα χρόνο στην Αϊόβα. Για τον αδερφό της, που λέει τον Σαμουράι Σίμπα, η ανασκόπηση του παλιού της ημερολογίου από εκείνη τη σύντομη χρονική περίοδο ήταν μεγάλη χαρά και τον ενέπνευσε να μοιραστεί μερικές σελίδες. Περιγραφόμενος στη σελίδα X του ως «ένας Ιάπωνας που αγαπά την Αμερική», του αρέσει να μοιράζεται «ιστορία…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Yuki was 16 years old, she was a Japanese exchange student for about a year in Iowa. For her brother, who goes by Samurai Shiba, looking through her old diary from that brief time period has been such a joy, and has inspired him to share a few pages. Self-described on his X page as “a Japanese guy who loves America ,” he enjoys sharing “stories, questions, history and laughs.” (He also adds that his stories are “inspired by real moments,” and notes that “details change.”) Looking back at one’s life through the earnest lens of a diary/journal can often be a delightfully eye-opening experience. Sometimes, we’re shocked at the things we once felt or might have said. And there are other times when we see, “Oh, yeah…I’m still this way.” For Yuki, it appears there were things she learned that she still carries to this day. A teen writes in her diary. Photo Credit: Canva In a post on X, Shiba shares, “My sister Yuki was an exchange student. She was terrified, so she kept a diary. Let me translate a few pages.” He then lays out the journal pages, which span from August of 1998 to June of 1999. ‘Proud of you kiddo’ “IOWA. 1998. AGE 16. Aug. 22 The host father is very big. He shook my hand very gently, like I was an egg. Aug. 25 Everyone on the road waves from their trucks. I do not know them. They do not know me. I wave back too late every time. Sept. 2 A teacher said “Great question!” My question was where the bathroom is. Sept. 14 The host mother writes notes in my lunch bag. Today: “Proud of you, kiddo.” I looked up “kiddo.” I am a kiddo now. Corn is the landscape View this post on Instagram Oct. 9 Corn is not a vegetable here. It is the landscape. Nov. 26 Thanksgiving. 23 people. Everyone said what they were thankful for. A cousin I met yesterday said, “Yuki.” My English left. I said thank you in Japanese. Dec. 31 I have not been homesick in a while. I think it is because this is also home. June 11, 1999 Going home tomorrow. The host father drove me past every field one more time. Every truck waved. Forever waving I waved back on time. Every one.” Shiba adds, “She’s 44 now. She still waves on time.” Some X commenters note that they too noticed how much corn there is in Iowa. One writes, “As a exchange student in 1996 I went to Iowa for 2 weeks and it is crazy how much corn there is.” Japanese prayer Another commenter shares that they laughed when hearing that Yuki’s teacher replied “great question” to her asking where the bathroom was. They also noted the Japanese meal blessing. “1. Sept 2 cracked me up. 2. I love the Thanksgiving reference. Yesterday I found a post about the Japanese meal blessing. I practiced saying “Itadakimasu” and “Gochisōsama deshita.” It’s going to take a LOT of practice, but it’s such a lovely way to start and end a meal, along with my prayer of thanks.” Shiba was impressed, writing, “You’re practicing ‘Itadakimasu’ and ‘Gochisōsama deshita’?! That made my whole day. Here’s a secret: most Japanese people mumble them so fast they sound like one word. If you say them slowly and clearly, you’ll already be more polite than half of Japan.” The post Japanese man shares sister’s 1998 diary when she was a 16-year-old foreign exchange student in Iowa appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

items.title: Πώς οι πιστώσεις άνθρακα βοήθησαν να ξεκλειδωθεί το Εθνικό Πάρκο Great Koala στη NSW
items.titleOriginal: How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Το Εθνικό Πάρκο του Μεγάλου Κοάλα μπορεί να ακούγεται σαν ένα μέρος που είναι πολύ καλό για να είναι αληθινό, αλλά είναι αληθινό. Μετά από περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία προεκλογικής εκστρατείας, τρεις πολιτειακές εκλογές και πάνω από 14 ώρες κοινοβουλευτικής συζήτησης, η Νέα Νότια Ουαλία δημιούργησε το δεύτερο μεγαλύτερο εθνικό πάρκο της πολιτείας. Αποτελείται από 478.000 εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made up of 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast. More than 100 species of flora and fauna will be protected within its boundaries. The park is a patchwork of existing protected areas stitched together with more than 178,000 hectares (roughly 440,000 acres) of former state forest and Crown Land. The legislation passed through approximately 160 amendments before it got there. The campaign started small. Conservationist Ashley Love began lobbying for the park after hearing from local residents that koalas in the region weren’t as common as they once were. “It became too much to ignore,” he said. What started as a proposal to protect Crown Land eventually became a Labor election platform. NSW Labor took it to the 2015 and 2019 elections, lost both, and won government in 2023 on a ticket that included the park. Carbon credits sealed the deal Carbon credits were central to making the legislation work. The federal Clean Energy Regulator registered a project covering more than 117,000 hectares (about 289,000 acres) of the park’s state forest areas. By formally ending native forest logging there, the government can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest , it turns out, generates more revenue than logged timber. Of course, that trade-off still has real costs. The Forestry Corporation of NSW had already cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour as the logging moratorium ate into forward orders. Timber NSW president Andrew Hurford laid it out: “Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter.” The government has committed to moving displaced Forestry Corporation staff into roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service. A park with gaps still to close NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe called it “a defining moment for conservation in NSW,” and by the numbers, it qualifies. Love, whose decade of advocacy made the proposal viable, was more measured. “Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward,” he said. Koalas need connected habitat to move, breed, and survive disease pressure. A 478,000-hectare patchwork is still a meaningful step up from what existed. The carbon credit structure gives the protected land a financial rationale that most past conservation campaigns lacked entirely. Love says he’ll keep pushing for the sections that didn’t make it in. After a decade, that sounds less like frustration than a habit he’s not planning to break. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Η μαμά δείχνει στο 9χρονο πώς να αφήνει τις άβολες συζητήσεις και είναι συμβουλή που πρέπει να ακούσουν όλοι
items.titleOriginal: Mom shows 9-year-old how to leave uncomfortable conversations and it’s advice everyone should hear
items.description: Λίγα πράγματα είναι πιο άβολα από το να κάθεσαι σαν ελάφι στους προβολείς ενώ κάποιος σε σπρώχνει σε μια απίστευτα αμήχανη συζήτηση. Είτε πρόκειται για συνομιλία TMI (υπερβολικά πολλές πληροφορίες) είτε θέλουν να μιλήσουν για πολιτική ή θρησκεία, είναι δύσκολο να πεις σε κάποιον ότι ένα θέμα είναι εκτός ορίων. Ωστόσο, σε μια viral ανάρτηση στο Instagram, η Charisse…
items.descriptionOriginal: Few things are more uncomfortable than sitting like a deer in the headlights while someone pushes you into an incredibly awkward conversation . Whether it’s a TMI (too much information) conversation or they want to talk about politics or religion , it’s hard to tell someone that a subject is off-limits. However, in a viral Instagram post, Charisse Sims makes an essential point about these awkward situations: it will be uncomfortable whether you tell them to change the subject or if you have to sit through the conversation. So, it’s better to take the option that’s less harmful to you. Sims is a mother of six and the host of the Parenting for the Culture podcast . She was also named a PBS KIDS Early Learning Champion in 2021 and is the founder of The Sims Library of Poetry . How do you leave uncomfortable conversations? She shared the advice while talking to her nine-year-old daughter, who she could tell felt very awkward about a recent conversation. “Immediately, when she started having that conversation, I could see on your face that you felt uncomfortable,” Sims told her daughter in an Instagram Reel. “When you have that feeling, your response to them should be, ‘I feel uncomfortable in this conversation. Let’s talk about something else.’” View this post on Instagram Sims then asked her daughter to repeat the phrase a few times to burn it into her brain for when she needed it. Her daughter then admitted that telling someone to change the conversation would be difficult. Most people probably agree that telling people you’d like to change the subject is uncomfortable. However, Sims makes a great point: you will be uncomfortable both ways, so choose the one that best suits you. “Which one is a longer discomfort, taking 10 seconds to say, ‘I feel uncomfortable in this conversation. Can we talk about something else?” Sims asked. “Or, sitting in a 20- to 30-minute conversation that you feel uncomfortable in?” A woman holding her hand out signaling “stop.” Photo credit: Canva “It is uncomfortable telling people stop. It is uncomfortable being like, ‘I don’t really like what you’re doing,’ because you’re worried you’re going to hurt their feelings, and you want them to like you,” Sims continued. “But it’s also uncomfortable to sit there and be uncomfortable for a long time. So choose your discomfort, and choose the one that’s going to help you, not hurt you.” An etiquette expert’s tip Candace Smith , an etiquette expert, says it’s also helpful if you have another topic on deck that the person may be interested in to make the transition smoother for both parties. “When you think it’s time to let the other person know you will change the subject, be positive, and smile. Keep your eye contact warm and direct,” she says , before giving an example: “I’m going to change our subject here. Let’s talk about something cool like the Marvel movie!” Sims’ advice is important because it’s something that all of us, adults included, could use next time we are forced into an uncomfortable situation. Her advice is a great tool for making sound decisions when we feel awkward and unable to think on our feet. “I wish when I was growing up, I was taught more how to navigate tricky situations rather than just being told to stay out of them,” Sims wrote in her post. “As simple as that is, it’s not always that easy. Our children need more support and actual practice navigating these awkward situations.” Child development experts agree that practicing assertive phrases through role-play helps kids use them in the moment, according to HuffPost and the Child Mind Institute .” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Mom shows 9-year-old how to leave uncomfortable conversations and it’s advice everyone should hear appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: 12 φωτογραφίες γυναικών πριν και μετά τον οργασμό ρίχνουν νέο φως στη σεξουαλική ευεξία των γυναικών
items.titleOriginal: 12 photos of women before and after an orgasm shines a new light on women’s sexual wellness
items.description: Μπορεί να θυμάστε το mega-viral project του Marcos Alberti « 3 Glasses » από το 2016, στο οποίο φωτογράφιζε ανθρώπους αφού είχαν καταναλώσει ένα, δύο και μετά τρία ποτήρια κρασί. Η σειρά ήταν εντυπωσιακή εν μέρει επειδή έδειξε τη σωματική μεταμόρφωση που προέρχεται από τη χαλάρωση μετά από λίγο κρασί. Η σειρά ήταν εντυπωσιακή εν μέρει επειδή δείχνει…
items.descriptionOriginal: You might recall Marcos Alberti’s mega-viral “ 3 Glasses ” project from 2016, in which he photographed people after they had consumed one, two, and then three glasses of wine. The series was impactful in part because it showed the physical transformation that comes from being relaxed after some wine. The series was impactful in part because it showed the physical transformation that comes from being relaxed after some wine. That, and it touched on a common curiosity. Haven’t we all wondered if we look as different as we feel after getting a little tipsy? (Spoiler alert: the answer is yes.) In 2017, using a very similar format to “3 Glasses,” as well as the elements of lightheartedness, novelty, and rawness that made it so special, Alberti used his photography to delve into a topic much less discussed: women’s sexual wellness. The concept is simple: photograph women before, during, and after an orgasm. You can see why he calls this the “O” project. What the project actually looks like Despite the subject matter, Alberti assures viewers that the intention wasn’t to be explicit, or even erotic, for that matter. The 20+ women who participated, of many ethnicities and nationalities, from countries seen as more sexually liberated (like the U.S. and France) to more conservative ones (like China and Singapore), were completely covered below the waist while using personal massagers. “The underlying message: all women deserve to be in control of their sexuality , no matter their background. Women should be free to be empowered by, and have a little fun with, their sexuality,” Alberti wrote on his website . Similarly, Fan Yang, then Global Brand Manager of Smile Makers (a sexual wellbeing brand that partnered with Alberti for this project) noted that the goal was to break through stigma and show female pleasure in a positive, healthy light. The hope is that society normalizes female pleasure, and that women feel free to connect with their own sexuality without shame or secrecy. Given that all the women who participated were “in awe” seeing themselves “glowing and radiant” in their final photo, as Yang put it, it feels safe to say mission: accomplished. Take a look: An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com An O Project participant. marcosalberti.com The behind-the-scenes video says it all In a video posted to YouTube, we get a behind-the-scenes look at Alberti’s process. Welcoming the models in, setting up his camera behind a curtain for privacy, talking them through the process, making them feel safe and comfortable, etc. We also get to see the “awe” that Yang spoke of. It’s palpable. “Initially, I was still apprehensive… [with] a lot of worry. And this one [referring to the final image] is like, ‘Ha! Life is beautiful!’” one woman shared, grinning ear to ear. Why this project matters beyond the photos We can talk at nauseam about how it’s a natural, vital part of a woman’s overall wellbeing, how research suggests it may be linked to less stress, better sleep, and more self-confidence (though some experts say the evidence is limited ), yada, yada, yada… but there’s nothing like actually witnessing its semi-miraculous powers firsthand. It’s one of the things that make photography so powerful. We feel something raw and honest on a visceral level, so that we can THEN talk about it with empathy and understanding. It’s clear that Alberti knows this on a deep level and is using that knowledge for something truly good. Be sure to follow Alberti ( @marcos_alberti ) on Instagram to keep up-to-date with all his work. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post 12 photos of women before and after an orgasm shines a new light on women’s sexual wellness appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο κωμικός εξηγεί τέλεια όλα όσα πρέπει να γνωρίζετε για το Gen X με τρεις μόνο λέξεις
items.titleOriginal: Comedian perfectly explains everything you need to know about Gen X in just three words
items.description: Ο Τζέισον Σάλμον έχει το δάχτυλό του στον παλμό ακριβώς για το τι κάνει τη Γενιά Χ. Αλλά με τον τυπικό τρόπο X, η δική του διαφημιστική σελίδα στο YouTube καυχιέται ότι «περιγράφεται σαν να παίρνει τις καλύτερες συμβουλές που έχεις πάρει ποτέ από τον πιο ανόητο άντρα που ξέρεις». Η ταπεινοφροσύνη του τον κάνει πολύ πιο γοητευτικό. Αλλά η αλήθεια είναι ότι αυτό που νομίζουμε δεν έχει νόημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Jason Salmon has his finger on the pulse of just what makes Generation X tick. But in typical X fashion, his own promotional YouTube page boasts that he’s been “described as like getting the best advice you’ve ever gotten from the dumbest guy you know.” His humility only makes him that much more charming. But the truth is, what we think doesn’t really matter to his X Generation. In his comedy special, Biscuits and Gravy , at one point, he asks the audience if there are any Gen Xers . A few people clap and cheer, and he responds, “Yeah. I don’t even care. That’s how Gen X I am. That’s a calling card to our generation.” @jsalmoncomedy Gen X would like you to leave us alone #genxtiktok #dontcare #genx #genxtiktokers #lucky #Standupcomedy #Jokes #fyp #CleanComedy #jasonsalmon ♬ original sound – Jason Salmon He points out the unlikelihood of a Gen Xer even being offended by that. “That’s not even dismissive to a Gen Xer. It’s like ‘I don’t care.’ ‘I don’t care, also. Nice to meet you.'” He then points to a person in the crowd and asks, “What generation are you?” But before they have a chance to answer, he jokes, “It doesn’t matter. I don’t care. That’s the beautiful thing.” He adds that if an audience member doesn’t like the joke, guess what? Doesn’t care. “If y’all don’t like this joke, guess what, you’re only giving me more cred as a Gen Xer. You’re only making me more powerful.” Gen Xers fought the ‘Battle of Who Could Care Less’ The truth is that some of the stereotypes about Gen X aren’t exactly true . Sure, director Richard Linklater’s film Slacker helped pin that label on us. And Ben Stiller’s film Reality Bites didn’t exactly help dissuade the argument that we were unprepared for adulthood. Gen X earned a reputation for apathy and ambivalence because it was skeptical of the status quo. In the ’90s, Gen X was often stereotyped as apolitical (even though, as Holmes notes in the same article, Gen Xers also brought a “chaotic and effective” kind of political organizing) and loved everything with a sense of irony. There was nothing less cool than being sincere, and credibility was king; there was nothing worse than being a sell-out or a poser. But in an October 2023 article called “ 8 Things That Gen X Gave the World ” (via The Arrow , via, gasp, the AARP website) Esquire editor at large and radio and television personality Dave Holmes dispels some of those myths. “Generation X is exactly like corn. We’re largely ignored in the broader culture, disregarded in polling, a demilitarized zone between the boomers and the millennials. But we’ve actually contributed a great deal to the society that has spurned us.” (Pew Research Center counted 65.2 million Gen Xers in 2019, compared with 72.1 million Millennials, and projected that Gen X would outnumber the Boomers by 2028.) Gen X made some big cultural contributions He goes on to list some of those contributions, which include, in part, blogs, alternative comedy, “comic books as our new global religion,” and a little something called the internet. Of the latter, he writes that in 1994, after he’d graduated from college and moved to New York, he had a friend who was “writing code for the Sony Music website.” He shares, “At the time, I had no idea what the word ‘website’ meant. My understanding of the internet came entirely from Prodigy, a rudimentary content delivery network. But then one Saturday afternoon, Mike and I went up to his office, he turned his monitor on, and after that 20-minute connection process, he opened Netscape and typed in ‘ https://www.yahoo.com .’ ‘There,’ he said, ‘search for anything.’ ‘Anything?’ I asked. ‘Anything at all. Someone will have made a website for it.'” So what can we say about Gen X now? So while apathy might not be the best description for Gen X, Jason Salmon proves one thing we can all agree on : they (we) have a sense of humor . Many of the comments agree. One commenter under his YouTube clips proves that maybe we DO care a little. “Why is Gen X trending so much lately? Are we finally getting the recognition that we don’t care about?” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Comedian perfectly explains everything you need to know about Gen X in just three words appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: J ust weeks after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at a college last September, students gathered in a University of Michigan classroom to discuss freedom of speech. Sitting in a semicircle, they were listening to one another share their views when one of the attendees pulled a red MAGA hat from his bag and asked if it would be okay to wear it. The gesture could have turned into a confrontation. The discussion’s moderator, however, said he was free to put it on. “We were all just like, ‘Okay, that’s your belief [and] that’s totally fine,’” recalls Sarah-Catherine Jackson, the president of BridgeUSA at UMich, the organization hosting the meeting. Students participate in a workshop at the BridgeUSA annual summit. Courtesy of BridgeUSA BridgeUSA at UMich is the University of Michigan’s chapter of BridgeUSA, a student movement built around structured political dialogue, welcoming different views as long as they are expressed with basic respect. Instead of debating for a quick win, students explain their beliefs, listen to others and stay in the room without needing to reach agreement. The need for such spaces is clear, says BridgeUSA. A 2024 Knight Foundation-Ipsos study of more than 1,500 college students between the ages of 18 and 24 found that two in three said they self-censored on topics such as gender, religion, race and LGBTQ+ issues during classroom discussions. A similar proportion reported that they believed such self-censorship limited educationally valuable conversations on campus. With another tense election pulling the country in opposite directions, BridgeUSA is betting that depolarization starts with something simple: getting supposed rivals to sit down and actually hear each other out. BridgeUSA — which was founded in 2017 at UC Berkeley after protests over a conservative speaker turned violent — works to facilitate those conversations. The organization has grown rapidly, from that first chapter in 2017, to 24 by 2020 , to 146 today. At its national summit in Philadelphia this August, 250 students gathered for leadership and moderation training, and to connect with peers from different regions and political perspectives. In spring 2024, pro-Palestine protests erupted at Columbia University in New York, leading to intensified disputes over campus speech, safety and protest, and prompting some to ask whether students with opposing views should engage with one another at all. BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel says that when the protests began, BridgeUSA only had a small presence at the university and no trained student leaders able to convene a dialogue. But a group of students believed that kind of conversation was sorely needed, so they established a BridgeUSA chapter and organized a discussion about Israel and Palestine, an event Meel says university administrators declined to support because they feared negative publicity. The students proceeded anyway, and within a year Bridge Columbia convened a gathering of at least 200 students. While considered successful, this experience highlighted BridgeUSA’s dependence on local leadership. BridgeUSA now emphasizes trying to support rapid-response dialogue immediately after campus violence, protests and other flashpoints where possible. Listening to political opponents takes courage on campuses where students feel pressure to demonstrate ideological loyalty, says Meel, adding: “I don’t think protest is any more courageous because everybody protests today.” Instead, he describes structured dialogue as “the new campus counterculture.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] While dialogue performs a distinct democratic function, says University of Virginia professor Rachel Wahl, who studies political dialogue, she is wary of setting conversation and protest against each other and asserts that public demonstration remains vital: “People who want to be in dialogue should consider protest an important form of political communication.” BridgeUSA plans to grow to 800 chapters (roughly a quarter of U.S. colleges) — a reach Meel says could help make dialogue a campus norm and give quieter students “social permission” to participate. To truly make an impact, Nicholas V. Longo, director of the Rutgers Democracy Lab, asserts that dialogue must also extend into the places and spaces where students already spend time. “Campuses need to not only engage students who are ready, but also students who might avoid these kinds of opportunities. We sometimes say we want to try to make engagement in dialogue unavoidable. To do this, we need to go to where students are at — in student centers, res life and first year experiences; but then also it’s essential to build these opportunities into the curriculum.” BridgeUSA CEO Manu Meel describes structured dialogue as the new campus counterculture. Courtesy of BridgeUSA Back at the University of Michigan, where chapter meetings typically draw 10 to 15 students, keeping conversations balanced takes deliberate effort. Jackson, a self-described fairly conservative student on a predominantly liberal campus, says executive board members with different political views review presentations and social posts for partisan framing, and flag language that appears to lean left or right. The midterms bring national stakes to Ann Arbor, the home of the university, where student turnout could help shape the outcome of the state’s competitive Senate race — and, with it, which party controls the chamber. But the measure of BridgeUSA’s success extends beyond election day, says Longo, who states that dialogue can build civic knowledge and lead to informed action. After the votes are counted, it can also help students “repair and rebuild” their communities, and work together, regardless of who wins. The post The Student Movement Addressing Campus Polarization Head On appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Cyclone Arnab turned Chhattisgarh’s sky blood red! But is it a warning sign or simply science? The answer lies in how sunlight travels through our atmosphere. Sunlight may look white, but it contains every colour. When the sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much longer stretch of atmosphere before reaching our eyes. Tiny particles in the air scatter shorter wavelengths, such as blue and violet, more strongly. Red and orange light travel through more easily, making sunsets appear dramatically colourful. During a cyclone, changing atmospheric conditions and increased moisture and airborne particles can influence how light scatters, creating striking red and orange skies. This phenomenon is connected to Rayleigh scattering, the science that helps explain why sunsets often appear red. So, a blood-red sky isn't automatically a bad omen or a danger warning. It's a fascinating reminder of how light and our atmosphere interact. Sometimes, what looks mysterious in the sky has a scientific explanation. #redsky #ScienceExplained #WeatherScience #Cyclone #Chhattisgarh #SunsetScience #Atmosphere #ScienceFacts #IndianWeather #NatureExplained #DidYouKnow #TheBetterIndia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.titleOriginal: For Generations, These Tamil Nadu Villages Have Gone Cracker-Free to Protect Bats
items.description: Σε μέρη του Ταμίλ Ναντού, το Diwali έρχεται με έναν ασυνήθιστο κανόνα: αφήστε τα κροτίδες έξω. Ο λόγος κρέμεται ανάποδα στα δέντρα. items.descriptionOriginal: In parts of Tamil Nadu, Diwali comes with an unusual rule: leave the firecrackers out . The reason hangs upside down in the trees. Hundreds of bats roost in village banyans and tamarinds. Rather than drive them away, residents have built traditions around protecting them. In some places, the custom is tied to a sacred tree or local deity. In others, it began with families feeding the animals. The stories are different, but the relationship is striking. These villagers do not see the bats as pests to chase away. They see them as neighbours, guests or even protectors, and have learnt to celebrate Diwali around their presence. The night shift that keeps nature growing When fruit bats leave their roosts after sunset, they begin a nightly journey in search of fruit and nectar. Their work, however, extends well beyond finding food. For generations, villagers have kept firecrackers away from their winged neighbours, protecting the bats that roost in their trees. All Photographs courtesy of: ( The Hindu ) As bats eat fruit, they disperse seeds across the landscape, helping plants regenerate in places where seeds might otherwise never reach. By feeding on nectar, some also pollinate flowers. These activities support the growth of trees and vegetation, which in turn provide food and shelter for other wildlife. Their daytime roosts are just as important. Large colonies often gather in the same trees, returning to familiar resting places after a night of foraging. Sudden, loud firecracker bursts and flashes of light can alarm bats and disturb their roosting behaviour. Repeated disturbance may cause them to abandon a tree and seek another place to rest. For the villages that share their landscape with these animals, keeping Diwali quiet is a simple way to reduce that disturbance. The family that climbed a tree to feed bats In Kazhuperumpakkam, near Vanur in Villupuram district, the story began with a tamarind tree. Families noticed bats gathering around it to feed on its fruit. Instead of driving them away, they began leaving food for the animals. The care went further. Men climbed the tree and placed a large vessel between its branches, filling it with water. Children watched the bats move around the tree and, as they grew older, continued the practice of feeding them. In Kazhuperumpakkam, a tradition of feeding bats grew into a community-wide effort to protect them. The village eventually took responsibility for protecting the animals. The panchayat banned firecrackers, and the practice continued even after the families who first cared for the bats moved away. The village has also faced a difficult side of conservation. Residents said the bat colony once numbered in the thousands, but hunting and disturbance led to a decline. The bats moved to another banyan tree after the old one lost branches. In Perambur, near Kollidam in Mayiladuthurai district, the relationship has a more spiritual connection. Hundreds of bats roost in a sprawling banyan tree called Vavvaal Thoppu , or the bat grove. A shrine dedicated to Lord Muneeswaran stands nearby, and residents consider the grove sacred. For more than a century, villagers have avoided firecrackers during Diwali. The festival is still celebrated, but residents gather at the Sri Aaladiamman temple instead of filling the night with fireworks. A father stopped his son from bursting crackers. Three generations followed. In Thoppupatti and Saampatti, in Tiruchirappalli district, hundreds of fruit bats roost in a large banyan tree near a statue of the village deity, Muniyappa Swamy. Residents believe the bats bring good fortune and protect the community. A father's decision to stop his son from bursting crackers in Kalapattu became a tradition carried forward through three generations. Dhanraj, a resident of Saampatti, told India Today that villagers avoid crackers because the noise disturbs the bats. He described watching them fly out in the evening and return by dawn as a sight that makes the village proud. In Kalapattu, near Katpadi, the custom has a personal memory attached to it. G Sampath recalled that when he was 12, his father stopped him from bursting crackers because bats roosted in the village's trees . The practice has continued for three generations. The village's protection goes beyond Diwali. Residents refuse to let outsiders catch or hunt the bats. Yet they make one exception: firecrackers are allowed during funeral ceremonies, when they are part of local rites. Sampath acknowledged that the noise may frighten the animals, but described it as unavoidable. Schoolchildren are learning to protect their winged neighbours At Kittampalayam, near Coimbatore, the effort to protect bats has reached the classroom. In November 2012, Government Middle School hosted a bat and bird conservation programme, introducing students to the animals that roost in their village. In Perambur, a sacred banyan tree shelters hundreds of bats, while residents celebrate Diwali without fireworks. The children learnt why bats matter and took part in an awareness rally alongside villagers, conservationists and personnel from a nearby Border Security Force base. The programme was part of a wider effort to protect a colony of around 2,000 Indian flying foxes that roosted in two banyan trees and a tamarind tree. Around 350 families had already agreed to avoid firecrackers during Diwali. The students helped carry that message beyond the school, encouraging the community to see the bats not as intruders, but as fellow inhabitants of the village. The programme gave children a way to connect what they learnt in class with the wildlife around their homes. By taking part in the rally, they helped carry the message beyond the school gates: protecting the bats meant protecting a part of their village that had shared its trees with them for generations. The bats are protected from crackers. But what about curious visitors? For these communities, protecting the bats also means guarding their roosts from hunting and disturbance. In Kazhuperumpakkam, villagers have spoken about outsiders catching bats. The community's decision to protect the roosts helps keep the animals from being treated as an easy target. At Kittampalayam, schoolchildren took the message of bat conservation beyond the classroom, encouraging hundreds of families to celebrate a quieter Diwali. In Kalapattu, residents have also refused to let outsiders catch or hunt the bats. Their protection is rooted in a custom passed down through generations, and in the belief that the animals belong in the village's trees. Perambur's Vavvaal Thoppu presents a different challenge. The banyan tree and its bats are closely tied to local belief, and some residents hope the grove can attract nature lovers. But visitors bring the possibility of noise and disruption. The question is how to welcome people without turning the bats' resting place into a spectacle. These villages have found a way to celebrate Diwali without asking their wild neighbours to leave. Sometimes, protecting wildlife begins with something as simple as choosing not to make a noise. Sources ' Choosing bats over fireworks: Coimbatore's Kittampalayam village leads the way this Deepavali too ': by Avantika Krishna for The Hindu, Published on 11 November, 2023 ' For over a century, these villagers have celebrated a noiseless Deepavali to protect bats ': by Express News Service for The New Indian Express, Published on 24 October, 2019 ' For this village in Tamil Nadu, it's bats over crackers on Deepavali ': by Antony Fernando for The New Indian Express, Published on 31 October, 2024 ' Tamil Nadu: These villages prefer silent Diwali to protect environment, bats and winged creatures ': by Lokpria Vasudevan for India Today, Published on 5 November, 2018

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

Τα τελευταία πέντε χρόνια, οκτώ μικρά και τρεις ενήλικες τίγρεις έχουν καταγραφεί εδώ, αυξάνοντας τις ελπίδες για αναπαραγωγικό πληθυσμό πέρα ​​από το Ranthamb…
items.descriptionOriginal: For nearly three decades, Rajasthan's Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary had no documented successful tiger breeding. Tigers passed through its forests, but could they raise cubs here again? That has finally changed. Over the past five years, eight cubs and three adult tigers have been recorded here, raising hopes of a breeding population beyond Ranthambore. The discovery is detailed in a new study by WWF-India and the Rajasthan Forest Department, released in Jaipur on 16 October 2026. What happens next matters. Why the birth of eight cubs matters Located in Rajasthan's Karauli district, Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary spreads across approximately 674 sq km of forests, rocky hills and deep ravines. Established in 1983, it forms the northern extension of Ranthambore Tiger Reserve. For tigers moving out of Ranthambore, these forests offer a route towards other wildlife habitats, including the Dholpur-Karauli Tiger Reserve and Madhya Pradesh's Kuno National Park. But a forest where a tiger can travel is different from one where it can raise cubs. A mother needs sheltered spaces to protect her young, enough wild animals to hunt and a suitable habitat where her cubs can grow. That is what makes the recent breeding records encouraging. They suggest that parts of Kailadevi are providing conditions in which tigers can reproduce. K C A Arun Prasad, Rajasthan's Chief Wildlife Warden, said, "Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary is emerging as a vital landscape for tiger conservation, with successful breeding after three decades." He believes protecting the forests and the routes connecting them could help establish a second breeding tiger population alongside Ranthambore. What 186 hidden cameras discovered To understand the wildlife living in Kailadevi, researchers from WWF-India and the Rajasthan Forest Department carried out a detailed assessment between November 2023 and February 2024. Striped hyenas were photographed most frequently among the larger meat-eating animals, followed by wolves and leopards Photograph: (WWF India) They collected usable records from 186 camera-trap stations placed across the sanctuary. These cameras automatically photographed animals passing through, helping researchers study wildlife that can be difficult to observe directly. The cameras recorded 27 mammal species, revealing the variety of animals sharing these forests. Among them were leopards. Researchers identified 29 individual leopards and estimated their density at approximately 3.65 per 100 sq km. Striped hyenas were photographed most frequently among the larger meat-eating animals, followed by wolves and leopards. Jackals, Indian foxes, jungle cats and caracals were also recorded. The team also studied plant-eating animals that serve as prey for tigers. Their numbers matter because breeding is only the beginning. As cubs grow, they need enough food and space to survive independently. Why these tigers need forests beyond Ranthambore As young tigers grow, they may leave their birth territories to find space of their own. For that journey, they need connected stretches of forest where they can move, find mates and establish new territories. This is where Kailadevi becomes particularly important. Its location helps connect Ranthambore with neighbouring wildlife habitats. But roads, expanding settlements and damage to forest patches can interrupt these routes, making movement difficult for animals. Conservationists will need to continue monitoring tigers, protecting forest connections and ensuring that enough wild prey remains available. Photograph: (Prashant Mahajan) Protecting these connections is therefore essential if Kailadevi is to support tigers over generations. And that work involves the people living around these forests. How nearby villages are helping protect the landscape WWF-India and Rajasthan Forest Department initiatives have benefited nearly 8,000 residents across 46 forest-fringe villages around Ranthambore and Kailadevi. These include livelihood support, cleaner energy options and programmes that involve people in protecting their surrounding forests. The aim is to meet local needs while reducing pressure on the habitat that wildlife depends on. Such work matters in places where people depend on the same forests that tigers and other wild animals need to survive. Can Kailadevi give these cubs a future? The return of tiger breeding is encouraging, but Kailadevi's recovery will depend on what happens next. Conservationists will need to continue monitoring tigers, protecting forest connections and ensuring that enough wild prey remains available. The eight cubs recorded over five years do not yet establish a secure, self-sustaining tiger population. They do, however, show why protecting this sanctuary matters. After nearly three decades without documented successful breeding , tigers are once again raising young in Kailadevi. With continued protection of its forests and support from the communities living around them, the sanctuary could become a home for future generations of tigers. Sources: 'New study finds Kailadevi Wildlife Sanctuary as a key stronghold for tiger recovery and wildlife conservation in Rajasthan' : WWF India Western India Conservation Landscape : WWF-India

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sensory Food Education for Children in UK Schools Helps Pupils Enjoy Vegetables Reading Time: 3 minutes Sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries is fully funded, helping pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. The charity TastEd now fully funds sensory food education for children in UK schools and nurseries. It helps pupils learn to enjoy fruit and vegetables. Teachers need no kitchen or fancy equipment. The need is clear. In the UK, 79.1% of children aged 5 to 10 eat fewer than 3.5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day. In a class of 30 pupils, that is about 24 children. Put another way, only about 21% of children in that age group reach 3.5 portions. TastEd wants to change that through food lessons, using sensory food education for children in UK schools nationwide. The charity is registered in England and Wales and in Scotland. Pressure has not solved the problem. TastEd says cajoling, reward charts and 5-a-day messages have not raised intake. The 5-a-day message urges 5 portions of fruit and vegetables daily. Yet the average UK child eats just over 1 portion of vegetables a day. Why do children eat so few? TastEd points to a simple reason. Many children dislike vegetables and don’t know them well. The charity shares telling examples. It says some British 11-year-olds have never tried a raw tomato. Some 8-year-olds cannot recognize an onion. Sensory food education for children in UK schools, as delivered by teachers, is simple in practice. A teacher brings fresh fruit or vegetables into the classroom. Children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear and taste. Children also say whether they enjoy the food. The setting is fun and pressure-free. TastEd says pupils often surprise themselves by enjoying foods they expected to dislike. TastEd calls taste education food education in its simplest form. It says the effect on children can be large. A course of lessons builds a taste for healthy foods and confidence in sharing preferences. Sensory food education for children in UK schools is simple in practice: a teacher brings in fresh fruit or vegetables, and children talk and write about what they see, smell, touch, hear, and taste in a fun, pressure-free setting. Photo by Yuliia Patrikhalkina on Pexels. The lessons follow the Sapere method. Many European countries have used it for decades. Evidence from Finland suggests children who receive taste education are more likely to try new vegetables, fruits and berries. The World Health Organization (WHO) backs a whole-school approach to healthy food. Its January 2026 guideline says healthy food in schools can help children build good eating habits for life. WHO estimates that 466 million children worldwide receive school meals. That fits the idea behind sensory food education for children in UK schools. Healthy habits begin early, and school is a practical place to start. Parents know the struggle. TastEd notes that giving children positive exposure to fruit and vegetables at home can be hard, especially with picky eaters. School lessons offer that exposure in a group setting. Schools also report that pupils become more adventurous with school lunches. That is a practical benefit for schools and families. Teachers get support, training and resources for sensory food education for children in UK schools. The lessons match the English National Curriculum and cover the food requirements of primary design and technology. They can also link to English, history and science. TastEd says the lessons need very few resources and no specialist knowledge. Any teacher can run them. The charity says its approach delivers the recommendations of the National Food Strategy, an independent review of England’s food system. Teachers share positive results. A reception teacher in Cambridge says the lessons build literacy skills and motivate pupils to write. A Lincolnshire teacher describes reluctant eaters becoming willing tasters over time. TastEd also explains why it is needed. It describes a worldwide child health crisis linked largely to diet. Fresh food can be costly, and some homes lack proper cooking facilities. The charity also notes that sugary foods are heavily marketed, while fresh home-made food is not. Classroom lessons give every participating child a chance to meet fresh produce. Parents and nurseries can join in too. Families can try at home with activities, lessons, and videos on the website. Activity clubs and childminders also have log-in options. Nurseries can use a dedicated page for the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS). EYFS is the framework for children from birth to age five in England. Primary schools have their own page. Other places are seeing similar results from fresh food in school. A statewide farm-to-school program in California now reaches 500 school districts and is a permanent policy. At one district, students line up for unfamiliar fruits such as rambutan. Primary schools and nurseries can sign up for sensory food education through the TastEd website. Access is fully funded. TastEd compares taste education to learning to read and write. It calls the skill food literacy, which helps children feel confident around food. What could sensory food education for children in UK schools change if every child learned it early? items.titleOriginal: The Tenderheart and the Roughneck
items.description: Ένας δημοσιογράφος πέρασε τον τελευταίο χρόνο της ζωής του ετοιμοθάνατου πατέρα του κάνοντας αυτό που έκανε πάντα με αγνώστους, αλλά ποτέ με τον άνθρωπο που τον είχε πληγώσει περισσότερο: κάνοντας πραγματικές ερωτήσεις και ακούγοντας χωρίς να πτοείται. Αυτό που αποκάλυψε -- σε ηχογραφημένες συνομιλίες, παλιές φωτογραφίες και δύο ξεπερασμένα κουτιά παπουτσιών κρυμμένα σε κοινή θέα -- ήταν ένα μοτίβο σύνθετων…
items.descriptionOriginal: A journalist spent the last year of his dying father's life doing what he had always done with strangers but never with the man who had hurt him most: asking real questions and listening without flinching. What he uncovered -- in recorded conversations, old photographs, and two weathered shoeboxes hidden in plain sight -- was a pattern of compounding grief, passed quietly from generation to generation: a boy who lost his father to a war, who then couldn't be a father, who raised a son he couldn't understand. "It's the kind of wound I now see can be passed, from generation to generation, from father to son," the writer reflects. The most devastating discovery came after his father died, when he opened the shoeboxes his father had begged him to burn -- love letters from a grandfather killed in Italy in 1944, full of tender plans for a boy he would never come home to raise. What the son found there wasn't an excuse for the distance between them, but something more rare: a reason, which turned out to be enough.

items.description: Στην κρύα, σε μεγάλο υψόμετρο περιοχή του Leh στο Ladakh, η γη που κάποτε θεωρούνταν άγονη, τώρα παράγει ένα από τα πιο ακριβά μπαχαρικά στον κόσμο. Οι πρώτες ανθοφορίες εμφανίστηκαν πρόσφατα στη γη…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the cold, high-altitude region of Leh in Ladakh, land once considered barren is now producing one of the world's most expensive spices. Saffron flowers have begun blooming here in less than 30 days after planting, offering fresh hope for agriculture in a region where farming conditions can be challenging. The first blooms appeared on land recently restored under Project Him Sarovar , an experimental initiative launched by Ladakh Lieutenant Governor VK Saxena. The most interesting part of the experiment is that the saffron flowers appeared much earlier than expected. The crop typically takes nearly two months to bloom after plantation, but the flowers in Leh appeared in less than half that time. The experiment could open up new opportunities for high-value crop cultivation in Ladakh, potentially creating additional income sources for farmers, local entrepreneurs, and young people. From barren land to a saffron field The experiment began on 1 October 2026, when nearly 800 kg of premium Iranian saffron corms were planted across 4,000 square metres of land in Leh. In the cold, high-altitude region of Leh in Ladakh, land once considered barren is now producing one of the world's most expensive spices. Photograph: (Instagram @moneycontrolcom) These corms, which are underground structures similar to bulbs, help saffron plants grow and produce flowers. The plantation involved around 90,000 corms, making it a substantial trial for the region. The land was previously degraded and unsuitable for cultivation. It was restored under Project Him Sarovar. The saffron plantation was then taken up to see whether the crop could grow in Ladakh's high-altitude conditions. Within weeks, the barren stretch of land began showing signs of life. Although the crop generally takes close to two months to flower after plantation, the first blooms appeared in Leh in less than 30 days. The first harvest brings encouraging results When Saxena visited the experimental field on Sunday, 1 November, he got to see the first flowers for himself. The field was producing an average of 20 to 25 blooming flowers each day. On the morning of his visit, the number reached 72, marking the highest daily count recorded so far. The team had also managed to collect nearly 22 grams of pure saffron over four days. While this is still a small harvest, it is an encouraging start for a crop being tested in a region where it has not traditionally been cultivated at this scale. The administration is now looking at how the plants perform under local conditions and whether the results can be sustained beyond this initial flowering period. Why saffron could be a valuable crop This crop is among the world's most expensive spices. It is widely used in cooking and traditional preparations, and its high market value makes it an attractive crop for farmers who can grow it successfully. India's saffron production is largely concentrated in Jammu and Kashmir, which accounts for approximately 90 percent of the country's total output. For farmers in Ladakh, cultivating saffron could offer another way to earn from their land. Instead of depending only on traditional agricultural practices, they could potentially grow a high-value crop with the opportunity to fetch better returns. The administration hopes the experiment will help diversify farming in the region, improve farmers' incomes and create opportunities for young people interested in agriculture and entrepreneurship. The experiment began on 1 October 2026, when nearly 800 kg of premium Iranian saffron corms were planted across 4,000 square metres of land in Leh. Photograph: (Instagram @moneycontrolcom) However, the project is still at the pilot stage. The first blooms are a positive sign , but further trials will be needed to establish whether the crop can be grown consistently and profitably on a commercial scale. Building on Ladakh's floriculture success This is not the first time the administration has experimented with high-value flower cultivation in Ladakh. Earlier, it undertook large-scale experiments with lilium and gladiolus in Leh. These flowers helped create livelihood opportunities for farmers, self-help groups, and local entrepreneurs. The success of these initiatives encouraged the administration to look at other crops that could grow in the region and offer better economic returns. Saffron is the latest addition to these efforts. If the ongoing trial proves successful, its cultivation could give local farmers another option beyond conventional crops and encourage the growth of small agro-based businesses. The Agriculture Department of the Union Territory of Ladakh and the field staff involved in the project have been acknowledged by the Lieutenant Governor for their work in bringing the experiment to life. For now, the 4,000-square-metre field in Leh offers an encouraging glimpse of what may be possible . Nearly 90,000 corms planted on restored land have already produced their first flowers, with the first saffron harvest following soon after. The field was producing an average of 20 to 25 blooming flowers each day. Photograph: (NDTV) Whether this experiment can eventually grow into a commercial farming opportunity remains to be seen. But for a region constantly finding ways to make agriculture more viable, these early blooms have given farmers and the administration something new to look forward to.
