items.description: Happy Eco News Το Παγκόσμιο Κίνημα Αποκατάστασης Εδάφους Φτάνει 4 Δισεκατομμύρια Άνθρωπους σε 193 Έθνη Χρόνος ανάγνωσης: 3 λεπτά Ένα παγκόσμιο κίνημα αποκατάστασης εδάφους, που ξεκίνησε μέσω ενός ταξιδιού με μοτοσικλέτα μήκους 30.000 χιλιομέτρων, έχει φτάσει περίπου 4 δισεκατομμύρια ανθρώπους και ωθεί τα έθνη σε πολιτικές που προστατεύουν το γεωργικό έδαφος από μη αναστρέψιμη υποβάθμιση.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations Reading Time: 3 minutes A global soil restoration movement, launched through a 30,000-kilometer motorcycle journey, has reached an estimated 4 billion people and is pushing nations toward policies that protect agricultural soil from irreversible degradation. Save Soil , the movement behind this global push, centers on a stark warning: soil with insufficient organic content essentially turns to sand, triggering cascading consequences for food security, water systems, biodiversity, and climate stability. Currently, 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are classified as degraded, a figure that underscores the urgency behind what has become one of the largest environmental awareness campaigns in recent history. The soil restoration movement was founded by Indian yogi and environmental activist Sadhguru, who embarked on a 100-day motorcycle journey spanning 27 countries and 30,000 kilometers from the United Kingdom to India to raise awareness. That journey became the foundation for a campaign claiming to have reached 4 billion people, roughly 60% of the world’s electorate, through 691 events and interviews, more than 8,970 media stories, and 50 iconic landmarks illuminated worldwide in support of the cause. At the core of the soil restoration movement is a specific, measurable goal: restoring at least 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil by shading land and enriching it with plant litter and animal waste. The movement outlines a three-pronged policy strategy presented at the UN Convention to Combat Desertification’s COP15: incentivizing farmers to increase soil organic matter, making carbon credits more accessible to farming communities, and establishing preferential marketing for produce grown in healthier, higher-organic-matter soil. The soil restoration movement aims to restore 3% to 6% organic matter in agricultural soil, which can hold up to 90% of its weight in water, addressing a crisis in which 52% of agricultural soils worldwide are already degraded. Photo by Tom Fisk on Pexels. The stakes extend across multiple interconnected crises. Degraded soils cannot adequately absorb and regulate water flows, contributing to droughts and floods alike, while organic-rich soil can hold up to 90% of its weight in water and release it gradually over time. Soil also stores roughly three times more carbon than living plants and twice as much as the atmosphere, meaning continued degradation risks releasing roughly 850 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, more than three decades of combined global emissions. The soil restoration movement has secured formal commitments from national governments through Soil Health memoranda of understanding, with countries including Azerbaijan, Romania, Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Suriname, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and the United Arab Emirates signing agreements committing to policies restoring and safeguarding soil health. The Caribbean region, in particular, has shown unified support, with multiple island nations joining within the same campaign cycle. Across North America, the soil restoration movement gained traction at the municipal level, with more than 150 cities proclaiming March 21 as Save Soil Day, including Washington, D.C., Austin, San Diego, Baltimore, Philadelphia, Phoenix, and dozens of smaller municipalities across the United States and Canada. These proclamations, while largely symbolic, reflect growing local government engagement with soil health as a civic priority rather than a purely agricultural concern. International institutions have also voiced support. The United Nations Environment Programme, the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization, the World Food Programme, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature have all publicly backed the soil restoration movement’s objectives, alongside the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture and the Commonwealth of Nations. The campaign explicitly compares itself to a previous global environmental success story: the 1987 Montreal Protocol, through which 197 countries agreed to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals after confirming the Antarctic ozone hole. That agreement eliminated 99% of ozone-depleting substances, and current projections suggest the ozone layer will fully recover by mid-century. The soil restoration movement positions this precedent as proof that coordinated international policy can reverse seemingly intractable environmental crises when sufficient public and governmental will exists. Beyond policy advocacy, the soil restoration movement has catalogued more than 1,000 sustainable soil management solutions spanning 193 nations, alongside engaging younger generations directly, with 3 million children reportedly writing letters to their national leaders advocating for soil health policies. Recent reporting connected to the movement has also highlighted soil degradation’s role as a driver of global migration, with projections suggesting human displacement could double by the century’s end as soil degradation, climate change, and food insecurity compound one another. Land-related conflicts have already played a significant role in most major wars across Africa since 1990, underscoring how soil health intersects with geopolitical stability far beyond agricultural productivity alone. As the soil restoration movement continues expanding its policy reach, its core argument remains consistent: thriving soil policies require public support, and public support requires sustained awareness. Whether this translates into a binding international framework like the one that reversed ozone depletion remains to be seen, but the scale of global engagement so far suggests soil health has moved from a niche agricultural concern to a mainstream environmental and public health priority. The post Global Soil Restoration Movement Reaches 4 Billion People Across 193 Nations appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: They Started by Picking Up Garbage. Now, Two Uttarakhand Schoolgirls Are Bringing Communities Together
items.description: Στο Pauri Garhwal του Uttarakhand, τα σκουπίδια στην άκρη του δρόμου ήταν δύσκολο να χαθούν. Αυτό που ήταν πιο εύκολο ήταν να το προσπεράσεις. Η Manvi Rawat και η Anshika Gaur, δύο μαθήτριες από την πόλη των λόφων, επέλεξαν μια διαφορετική απάντηση. Αντί να περιμένουν κάποιον άλλο να καθαρίσει, άρχισαν να μαζεύουν μόνοι τους τα σκουπίδια. Οι προσπάθειές τους δεν τους κέρδισαν αμέσως…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Pauri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, the garbage on the roadside was difficult to miss. What was easier to do was walk past it. Manvi Rawat and Anshika Gaur, two schoolgirls from the hill town, chose a different response. Instead of waiting for someone else to clean up, they began picking up litter themselves. Their efforts did not immediately win them support. People mocked them for what they were doing, turning a simple attempt to clean their surroundings into a test of whether they would continue despite the criticism. They did. What began as a small cleanup effort grew into Pauri Eco Warriors, a student-led environmental initiative that brings young people together to tackle litter and plastic pollution. Today, the group has grown beyond its two founders, with more than 40 student members and around 15 to 18 volunteers participating in each cleanup drive. Their work has also moved beyond collecting waste. Through plantation initiatives, sapling distribution, and Maulyaar, a community festival built around environmental action, Manvi and Anshika are working to make conservation a shared responsibility rather than an occasional activity. From being mocked to building a movement The problem the two students responded to is familiar across Indian towns and cities. Plastic wrappers, disposable packaging and other waste accumulate in public spaces, along roadsides and near waterways. In mountain regions, where settlements and natural landscapes exist side by side, litter can become an environmental concern that extends beyond the place where it is discarded. For Manvi and Anshika, the first step was to address the waste they could see around them. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) Their decision was not necessarily the easiest one to make. The mockery they faced illustrates one of the social barriers that can discourage people from participating in community work. Why cleaning a hill town matters Pauri Garhwal's landscapes are part of a larger mountain environment in which forests, rivers, settlements and roads are closely connected. Waste left in public spaces can be carried by rainwater into drains and waterways, while discarded plastic can persist in the environment long after the person who dropped it has left. Cleaning up litter helps remove waste already present, but it cannot prevent the problem from recurring on its own. Pauri Eco Warriors has sought to build on this idea by combining cleanup drives with plantation activities , sapling distribution and environmental awareness campaigns. Its stated mission is to protect the district's mountains, forests and rivers through community-led conservation and more sustainable practices. Maulyaar: taking conservation beyond cleanups The founders have also taken their efforts into community events through Maulyaar, a festival that brings together activities such as environmental runs, plantation drives, cleanups, and awareness campaigns. Through plantation initiatives, sapling distribution, and Maulyaar, a community festival built around environmental action, Manvi and Anshika are working to make conservation a shared responsibility rather than an occasional activity. Photograph: (Pauri Eco warriors) Environmental awareness, after all, is not only about knowing that plastic pollution is harmful. It is also about translating that knowledge into habits and collective action. What happens after the cleanup? Pauri Eco Warriors' stated achievements extend beyond its regular student group. The initiative reports more than 10,000 trees planted, over 15 rivers cleaned, more than 500 active volunteers, over 25 events organised, activities across 30-plus villages and five awards received. These figures point to an effort that has grown beyond the founders' original cleanup drives. For Manvi and Anshika, the journey from being mocked for picking up garbage to building a student-led initiative offers a reminder that community action can begin on a small scale. It does not replace the responsibility of local authorities to provide effective waste management , but it can bring more people into the effort to protect the places they share. Sources: 'Protecting-Our Mountains,Our Future' : Pauri Eco Warriors

items.description: Τον Νοέμβριο του 2022, όταν ο Bharat Sisodia και η ομάδα του έφτασαν σε μια τοποθεσία στο Ahmedabad, βρήκαν ένα αιωνόβιο δέντρο peepal που είχε ήδη κοπεί. Αλλά ο Bharat ήθελε να μάθει αν οι ρίζες του ήταν ακόμα ζωντανές. Εάν en…
items.descriptionOriginal: In November 2022, when Bharat Sisodia and his team reached a site in Ahmedabad, they found a century-old peepal tree that had already been cut down. Only about six to seven feet of its trunk remained. For a tree that had stood there for nearly 100 years, it seemed like the end. But Bharat wanted to find out whether its roots were still alive. If enough of the root system had survived, perhaps the tree could grow again. What followed was an ambitious rescue. His team dug around the tree, brought in a 50-tonne crane and carefully moved what remained of it nearly two kilometres to another location. There, they replanted it in a specially prepared pit and continued caring for it as it recovered. The peepal has since reportedly begun showing new growth. The soil that travels with the tree's roots also plays a role in transplantation, helping the root system retain some of its original growing environment. Photograph: (Videograb-Catch Foundation) For Bharat, this was a reminder of something he has believed for years: planting a tree is only the beginning of the responsibility we have towards it. Since 2014, he has been working on an idea he calls 'plantenance', a combination of planting and maintenance. It focuses on giving trees the care they need to survive and grow, whether they have just been planted or have been standing for decades. At a time when roads, buildings and other infrastructure are reshaping our cities, his work raises an important question. When an old tree stands in the way of development, can we find a way to save it? Speaking to The Better India , Bharat shares what went into rescuing the peepal, why moving a mature tree requires such careful planning, and what cities can do to protect the trees they already have. Could a century-old tree survive after being cut down? When Bharat and his team arrived at the site, their first concern was the tree's roots. A tree that has been cut back so severely cannot simply be lifted out of the ground and replanted with the expectation that it will survive. Its chances of recovery depend on how much of its living root system remains intact and whether it can cope with the disturbance of being moved. The team began by digging a trench approximately six feet deep around the peepal. They then used water to soften the surrounding soil, making it easier to carefully free the roots. Moving a tree of this size required heavy machinery, manpower and careful preparation. A 50-tonne crane was brought in to lift the tree, which was then transported nearly two kilometres to its new location. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) At the new site, the team had prepared a planting pit with soil treatments and nutrients to support the tree's recovery. Once it was replanted, they continued looking after it. That care was especially important because the move had placed the tree in unfamiliar ground. Its roots would have to recover and establish themselves again so they could draw enough water and nutrients from the soil to support new growth. Several factors could influence its recovery, including the tree's condition before transplantation, the extent of damage to its roots and the weather in the weeks that followed. For Bharat, getting the peepal safely into the ground was an important first step. The next challenge was helping it stay alive. Why Bharat believes planting a tree is only the first step Every year, tree-planting drives bring thousands of new saplings into our cities and neighbourhoods. But how many of those saplings are still alive a few months later? A newly planted sapling needs regular watering, suitable soil, the right seasonal conditions and continued attention. Without that care, even a promising plantation drive can struggle to produce healthy, mature trees. Bharat believes the same responsibility applies when an existing tree is moved. He calls this approach 'plantenance', bringing planting and maintenance together so the focus remains on a tree's long-term survival. "An important part of plantenance is understanding what a tree needs after it has been planted or transplanted," he explains. Unlike moving an ordinary object from one location to another, transplanting a tree means disturbing a living root system that has spent years growing into its surroundings. The recovery process can take weeks or months, depending on the tree's condition and the weather. According to Bharat, favourable monsoon conditions can help a transplanted tree recover. Its roots may need at least two months to begin rebuilding, although the actual time depends on how much of the original root system remains intact and the damage it has sustained. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bharat Sisodia (@bharatsisodiaofficial) Protecting the main root system is especially important. If those roots are badly damaged during excavation or transportation, the tree may struggle to absorb the water and nutrients it needs. This is why his team assesses the condition of each tree before deciding how to dig around it, lift it and transport it. And because every tree is different, the same method cannot be applied to every rescue. How far can an old tree be moved safely? Finding a suitable new home for a mature tree requires just as much thought as moving it there. When Bharat and his team plan a transplantation, they generally look for a site within the same region, preferably close to where the tree originally stood. Depending on the circumstances, they may move a tree around 10 kilometres. In some cases, the distance can extend to 15 to 20 kilometres. The aim is to find a location where the tree has a reasonable chance of adapting and growing again. Keeping the move relatively local can help because the environmental conditions are likely to be more familiar. The soil that travels with the tree's roots also plays a role in transplantation, helping the root system retain some of its original growing environment . "Understanding the environment is essential," Bharat says. The month, weather and temperature all need to be considered, along with the tree's condition and the suitability of its new location. A crane may make it possible to move a mature tree, but its future depends on what happens before and after the move. The Ahmedabad peepal is one example of how Bharat's team approaches a damaged tree. Another incident, involving a fallen banyan tree on Ahmedabad Airport Road, shows why he believes protecting trees must begin with the conditions in which they grow. When concrete leaves a banyan tree struggling to grow Banyan trees are known for their spreading branches and extensive root systems. As they mature, aerial roots grow down from their branches towards the ground. Over time, some of these roots develop into additional supporting trunks, helping the tree spread and support its growing canopy. But in cities, the space around a tree is often covered with concrete or other hard surfaces . Bharat recalls a banyan tree that had fallen on Ahmedabad Airport Road. When his team examined the site, they found that the cemented surroundings had restricted the development of its aerial roots. The tree had been growing in an environment where the roots that could have helped support its weight had limited room to develop. According to Bharat, his team eventually removed the fallen tree from the site, and he describes the operation as successful. The incident highlighted a problem that extends well beyond one banyan tree. For a mature tree, the space beneath and around the ground matters as much as the branches and leaves we see above it. Photograph: (Catch Foundation) "Compacted soil, sealed surfaces and inadequate space can affect root development. When the conditions that support a tree's growth are compromised, its long-term stability and health may also be affected," he shares. For a mature tree, the space beneath and around the ground matters as much as the branches and leaves we see above it. And once a tree becomes unstable or falls, rescuing it can require a much larger effort . In Vasai, saving trees became a community effort Bharat's work has also taken him beyond Ahmedabad. In Vasai, Maharashtra, he says his team helped relocate nearly 50 trees that were facing removal in connection with work by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The effort required machinery and manpower, along with the involvement of people living in the area. Local residents and leaders participated in the work, and the team hired people from the community to help with the transplantation. For Bharat, their involvement made an important difference. "Community involvement is really important," he says. "When we have to transport trees, we need people to help. Local residents can make a real difference." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bharat Sisodia (@bharatsisodiaofficial) Moving a mature tree involves digging around its roots, carefully lifting it, arranging transportation, preparing the new site and ensuring that it receives the care it needs afterwards. Having local people participate makes it possible for the community to contribute directly to protecting the trees around them. It also reflects the thinking behind Bharat's idea of plantenance: keeping trees alive is an ongoing responsibility that people can share. Can a newly planted sapling replace a 100-year-old tree? A mature tree has spent decades growing its roots and canopy. In that time, it has become part of its surroundings, providing shade, supporting birds and other wildlife, and contributing to the biodiversity of the area. Planting a new sapling is valuable, but that young tree will need years to grow and begin providing many of the same benefits. Bharat also recognises that moving an old tree comes with its own limitations. "Their ecological functions cannot be replicated immediately by planting a young sapling in their place. Equally, transplanting a mature tree does not automatically preserve all the ecological benefits it provided at its original location," he adds. The rescue of the Ahmedabad peepal offers an example of what may still be possible after a tree has suffered severe damage. But Bharat does not believe that every felled tree can necessarily be saved. Much depends on its condition, the health of its roots and the care it receives during and after transplantation. For India's growing cities, the larger challenge lies in preventing mature trees from reaching that point. Planning roads and buildings around existing trees, leaving enough room for roots to grow, providing suitable planting conditions and ensuring long-term maintenance can all help protect the greenery already present in our neighbourhoods. The century-old peepal in Ahmedabad was given another chance after it had been cut down. Its rescue leaves us with a question worth asking whenever an old tree stands in the path of development: could we give it the space and care it needs to keep growing right where it is?

Τα συμβατά μοντέλα αναμένεται να h…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM California just gave apartment renters a shot at solar. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill legalizing plug-in solar panels, also called balcony solar, clearing the way for a technology that doesn’t require a roof you own, a contractor, or tens of thousands of dollars up front. Compliant models are expected to hit shelves in mid-2027. How the hardware works The hardware is minimal: a few small panels, an inverter, and cables. The panels can hang from a balcony railing, mount outside a window, or sit in a backyard. Existing models run from $300 to $2,200 , much cheaper than a rooftop installation because you set them up yourself. In Germany , where they’re already common, you just plug them into a wall outlet. California’s version has more certification requirements for now, but that’s where the law is pointed. Who is historically left out of rooftop solar? Rooftop solar has always had prerequisites. You need to own your home, have a qualifying roof, and either have capital or qualify for financing. That locked out renters from day one, along with a lot of low-income households and anyone in a multifamily building. “These small, easy-to-use solar panels will give everyone, including renters, the relief they desperately need on our outrageous energy bills,” said state Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote the bill. It passed with bipartisan support. The benefits of plug-in A plug-in system can cover up to 20 percent of a home’s electricity needs and save as much as $500 a year for a small apartment. California electric bills have climbed hard over the past few years, so that number means something to a lot of people. The registration overhaul The registration change matters nearly as much as the legalization. Under the old rules, adding a plug-in panel meant completing the same interconnection paperwork required for a full rooftop system, which could cost up to $800 and take days. Advocates noted that process cost more than the panels themselves in some cases. Under the new law, registration is free and immediate. Systems must stay under 1,200 watts per home, pass third-party safety certification, and include protection against backfeeding electricity into the grid during outages. Products currently on the market don’t meet those standards yet, so the old registration process still applies for now. The sale of non-compliant systems becomes illegal in 2030, and the law runs from 2027 to January 1, 2030. “The market is sending a clear signal to manufacturers that they need to develop a California system,” said Cora Stryker, co-founder of Bright Saver, a plug-in solar advocacy group. California is the tenth state to pass this kind of law. Utah went first in March 2025; Colorado, Virginia, and Maine followed. But California is the country’s largest electricity market, which means manufacturers pay attention in a different way. What advocates have been describing for years, plug-in solar on the shelf at a hardware store, is now a reasonable near-term prospect. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Italian federation of pediatricians designed a box of games to help parents ask their kids how their day went. Let’s think about this for a minute. A medical organization had to build a conversation starter for families at dinner because something else kept stealing away everyone’s attention. Fifteen restaurants across Sardinia are running a one-month pilot called A tavola senza schermi , “at the table without screens.” Families who come in are asked to put their phones away. In exchange, staff hand over a “reunion kit,” a pediatrician-designed box with games, drawings, and prompts for parents and kids to work through together. The thinking behind the program The scheme is the work of Anna Cau, Sardinia’s children’s ombudsman, a former juvenile magistrate who partnered with the island’s restaurant federation to make it happen. The 15 restaurants joined voluntarily. Ultimately, the plan is to expand on the same basis. Cau is deliberate about how she describes the initiative. “The idea is not to rely solely on prohibitions or to place the burden of responsibility entirely on parents, but to ensure our broader environment supports parents in their role and helps minors integrate with others,” she said. The usual framing for children’s screen time puts the entirety of the problem on parents: their choices, their habits , their failures, their job to fix. Cau is coming at this issue from a different, more holistic angle. She wants the places families actually move through to be part of the answer rather than indifferent to the question. What restaurant owners notice Emanuele Frongia, president of the Sardinian restaurant federation, described what pushed the conversation forward. Families come in and sit down together, but within a few minutes, the talking stops. “We increasingly observe that during these moments lively chatter is replaced with stretches of silence as people look at their devices,” he said. “Often a child is handed one to keep them quiet.” It’s that last part that we really need to sit with and consider. The phone at the family table isn’t always something a kid reaches for. In fact, sometimes it’s a parent who puts it in their hands. The table in Italy isn’t just where you eat. It’s where the work of being a family gets done: the catching up, the arguing, the unremarkable talking that makes people feel known to each other. What Cau and the restaurant owners around her are watching is that shift happening meal by meal, as the phone becomes easier to reach for than whatever the silence might turn into. The real power of the reunion kit The reunion kit is both the sweetest part of this initiative and the most honest. It’s a concession that stepping away from screens needs a little structure to start. Most families handed a box of games by a waiter will end up talking without consulting the instructions. The box matters because without it, the phones inevitably come back out, at least for now. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: In an Oct. 28 letter from the editors , Life Magazine — which was founded in 1936 and became an icon of visual storytelling — announced it will begin publishing again after nearly 20 years. Its first new print issue “offers a window into an America searching for meaning.” That 250-page edition hits newsstands Nov. 23, The New York Times reported , the inaugural step forward in a revival made possible by Bedford Media’s acquisition of the publication in 2024. The holding company was founded the year prior by model Karlie Kloss and is co-owned by her husband, venture capitalist Joshua Kushner. More than 120 people put together the forthcoming issue, focusing on “finding the ordinary in the extraordinary, and the extraordinary in the ordinary,” per the editors’ letter. The reincarnated brand will expand into other avenues as well, amplifying its quarterly print pieces through digital storytelling, documentaries, and events. © CORBIS—Corbis/Getty Images When Henry Luce founded Life , at the tail end of the Great Depression and three years before World War II began, the intent was to “harness the emerging power of photojournalism,” the letter reads. Luce had co-created Time magazine 13 years prior to deliver a concise weekly news digest to busy readers. Life took an opposite approach, inviting Americans to pore over dramatic multi-page photo spreads and essays that told stories about 20th-century topics large and small: from groundbreaking science and civil rights to movie stars and the lives of everyday people. The first issue came out Nov. 23, 1936 ( you can scroll through it in its entirety online ). The cover story captured one of the major public works projects in development under then-President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s historic New Deal, and Page 2 featured a photo of a baby held upside down by a doctor moments after birth. RELATED: Gordon Parks: How Life Magazine’s First Black Staff Photographer Shed Light on Social Justice With Expressive Images That view into the miracle of life (no pun intended) likely felt unprecedented to readers at the time. The newborn was George Story, who went on to become a journalist and liked to joke at parties that a nude picture of him had once been published in a national magazine. Santi Visalli/Getty Images After nearly four decades, Time Inc. ceased weekly publication of Life in 1972, citing production costs. The magazine returned in 1978 as a monthly publication and ran until 2000. In a full-circle moment, its final issue in that format also featured Story — this time covering his death at age 63. It was resurrected again in 2004 as a weekly newspaper supplement, but shut down three years later due to a decline in newspaper readership and ad sales, the company said, per NBC News. The upcoming revival marks exactly 90 years since Life began. Take a look back at some of its most iconic photos and covers. items.descriptionOriginal: “Nobody can love that face.” Today, she’s a finalist in Miss India Uttar Pradesh. ❤️ Born with a port-wine stain on her face, she grew up facing stares, cruel comments and bullying. At school, children told her she was weird and refused to sit with her. The hurt followed her everywhere. She began skipping school, avoiding photographs and hiding from people. There was a time when she couldn't even look at herself in the mirror. Then her sister encouraged her to do something that terrified her: stand in front of a camera. With her sister by her side, she slowly began creating content and exploring modelling. Even when online trolls called her ugly, she stopped trying to fit into someone else's definition of beauty. The girl who once avoided cameras is now a Miss India Uttar Pradesh finalist and has won the People's Choice Award. Today, people reach out to tell her that her journey has helped them embrace themselves. She isn't celebrated because she overcame a visible difference. She's celebrated because she refused to let prejudice decide how much space she deserved to take up. Her face was never something to be ashamed of. And now, she wants others to know that they never have to hide theirs either. ❤️ #MissIndiaUttarPradesh #PortWineStain #BirthmarkAwareness #SelfLove #BodyPositivity #BeautyBeyondAppearance #StopBullying #Confidence #PageantJourney #BreakingStereotypes #Acceptance #WomenWhoInspire #RealBeauty #InspiringStories #TheBetterIndia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. On the forested edges of Shillong, a camera trap recorded an animal that is rarely seen, even by those who study wildlife. Moving through the forest under the cover of darkness was a Chinese pangolin, a critically endangered mammal that has now been documented in the Wildlife Institute of India's (WII) study area in Meghalaya for the first time. The sighting is significant for more than the presence of a threatened species. Forests bordering urban areas may appear small compared with protected wilderness, but they can provide vital shelter for animals facing habitat loss and fragmentation. A rare visitor, recorded on camera The record emerged from WII's ongoing project, Assessment of Mammalian Assemblages in Meghalaya, which focuses on the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests along Shillong's urban edges . "This rare record comes from our ongoing project," the institute said, highlighting the first documentation of the Chinese pangolin within its Meghalaya study area. 🌿 A Milestone record on the Fringes of Shillong! 📸✨ Our camera traps have recorded the Critically Endangered Chinese Pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) for the very first time in our study area! 🛡️🐾 This rare record comes from our ongoing project "Assessment of Mammalian Assemblages in Meghalaya", focusing on the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests right on the urban edges of Shillong. These peri-urban city forests harbor a remarkably unique and diverse assemblage of wildlife. Alongside the Chinese pangolin, our cameras captured iconic species including the Large Indian Civet, Leopard Cat, Masked Palm Civet, Yellow-throated Marten, Indian Crested Porcupine, and Kalij Pheasant. 🌲 Why This Matters: Urban-adjacent and city-fringe forests are often overlooked, yet they act as critical ecological refuges for species threatened by habitat fragmentation and urban development. Finding a Critically Endangered specialist like the Chinese pangolin sharing space with a rich suite of carnivores and small mammals proves that these urban forest patches are invaluable biodiversity strongholds that must be strictly protected and preserved. 👥 @Himalayanwolf1 @lifeofawild @nishinath @supratikroy @meghalayaforest @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) October 20, 2026 The finding is particularly valuable because systematic information about the species' population and distribution across parts of Northeast India remains limited. Although the Chinese pangolin is known to occur in the region, there is little recent systematic data on its status and numbers. A camera-trap record does not, by itself, establish how many pangolins live in these forests or whether their population is stable. However, it confirms the species' presence in the study area and provides researchers with an important starting point for further monitoring. What makes the Chinese pangolin special? Pangolins are nocturnal insectivores, meaning they are active mainly at night and feed on insects. Their bodies are covered in overlapping scales, and when threatened, they curl into a tight ball, using their armoured exterior as protection. Yet these defences offer little protection against people. Pangolins are widely recognised as the most trafficked mammals in the world, making their survival a major conservation concern. Forests bordering urban areas may appear small compared with protected wilderness, but they can provide vital shelter for animals facing habitat loss and fragmentation. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust of India) Of the world's eight pangolin species, two are found in India: the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) and the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata). The Chinese pangolin is native to parts of the northern Indian subcontinent, northern Southeast Asia and southern China. In India, it occurs across northeastern states and northern West Bengal. Arunachal Pradesh is considered one of its strongholds. The species has been listed as Critically Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List since 2014, reflecting its severe risk of extinction in the wild. Can you tell the two Indian pangolins apart? Although both species are covered in protective scales, there are some distinguishing features: Scale size: The Chinese pangolin has smaller scales than the Indian pangolin. Tail: The Indian pangolin has a terminal scale on the underside of its tail. This scale is absent in the Chinese pangolin. Scale weight: The dry weight of scales from one Chinese pangolin is roughly 500–700 grams, compared with approximately 1.5–1.8 kg for an Indian pangolin. These differences can help distinguish the two species, though identifying an animal in the wild requires careful observation. More than a pangolin The Chinese pangolin was not the only animal recorded during WII's camera-trap study. The institute documented a range of other wildlife in the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests, including the Large Indian Civet, Leopard Cat, Masked Palm Civet, Yellow-throated Marten, Indian Crested Porcupine and Kalij Pheasant. The presence of several mammals and birds also makes these sites valuable for understanding how different species use habitats close to human settlements. WII has described these peri-urban forests as harbouring a remarkably unique and diverse assemblage of wildlife. Why Shillong's forests matter Urban forests are often valued for their role in improving the quality of life for people, from providing green spaces to supporting local ecological processes. But their importance also lies in the wildlife they sustain, including species that may otherwise go unnoticed. "Finding a critically Endangered species like the Chinese pangolin sharing space with a rich suite of carnivores and small mammals proves that these urban forest patches are invaluable biodiversity strongholds that must be strictly protected and preserved," WII said. Protecting these forests will require recognising them as wildlife habitats, not simply undeveloped land around a city. Sources: 'Wildlife forensics helps cause of pangolins' : By Aswathi Pacha , Published on 8 May 2021 'Indigenous knowledge to track and save the Chinese pangolin' : By Nikhil Sreekandan, Published on 17 December 2025

Ήταν μια μικρή ομολογία, αλλά έφερε το βάρος μιας επιδημίας. Σε όλες τις πανεπιστημιουπόλεις των ΗΠΑ,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere between the gorges and botanic gardens of Cornell University's campus, a student on a guided nature walk looked up from hours of screen time and said something that stopped the walk leader cold: "This is the first time I've actually touched grass." It was a small confession, but it carried the weight of an epidemic. Across U.S. campuses, colleges are turning to "social prescribing" -- a practice borrowed from the UK where physicians write actual referrals, logged in electronic health records, for time in nature, art, movement, or community -- as a complement to counseling and medication for the surging mental health crisis among students. At Cornell, over 2,200 students received nature prescriptions last year, and 88 percent reported an improved mood. At Stanford, a dedicated care navigator connects students to pottery classes, dance workshops, and live performances -- and 80 percent of those who attended reported better mental health. What these programs are quietly surfacing is something older than any diagnosis: that belonging, beauty, and the sensory world are not luxuries but medicine. The student who finally touched grass wasn't being dramatic. She was describing a kind of return.

items.descriptionOriginal: For the children gathered around her, a patch of sand becomes their first writing book, and their fingers become pencils. At 85, Indira Amma from Kerala is introducing young learners to the world of letters through a traditional method passed down through generations. For the past decade, she has reportedly been teaching children Malayalam , Hindi, English, and mathematics using this humble approach. Instead of beginning with notebooks and pencils, she lets children trace letters in sand, helping them become familiar with the alphabet through touch and practice. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mom of Safachiiii 🤍 (@mom_of_safaachiiii) Her method draws on Kerala's tradition of Ezhuthiniruthu, a ceremony that marks a child's introduction to learning. Traditionally associated with Vijayadashami, the ritual involves guiding children to trace their first letters in rice or sand. The act symbolises the beginning of their educational journey. An endearing glimpse of this tradition shows Ashaatti Ammumma patiently teaching hindi alphabets to young children at the Temple of English School. As the children follow along, each letter becomes an opportunity to learn through practice, guided by her gentle approach. For young children, learning to recognise and write letters takes patience and repetition . Tracing them in sand offers an experiential way to understand their shapes, allowing little learners to practise each movement as they grow more confident. What makes this approach special is how it connects everyday learning with a tradition strongly rooted in Kerala's cultural heritage. At a time when classrooms are embracing digital tools, it is a reminder that learning need not always begin with a screen or expensive resources. Sometimes, all it takes is a handful of sand, someone willing to guide a child's hand , and the time to let them learn at their own pace. Through this practice, Indira Amma is helping keep a traditional way of learning alive while giving young children a meaningful start to their educational journeys.

items.descriptionOriginal: Do you tend to experience jealousy, have difficulty trusting people, or resist emotional intimacy out of fear? While genetics can play a role in qualities like these presenting themselves, they may also be explained by attachment theory: the idea that our earliest relationships influence how we’ll connect with people later in life. “As children, we build our understanding of relationships based on our caregivers,” Jennifer Rolnick , a licensed clinical psychologist and co-owner of Watch Hill Therapy, told Nice News. “If a caregiver is consistently supportive, a child learns that relationships are safe. If a caregiver is inconsistent, distant, or intimidating, a child learns defense mechanisms in order to survive.” These early, deeply ingrained patterns shape how we read people, manage conflict, and regulate emotions, resulting in specific “attachment styles” that we hold onto into adulthood, Rolnick explained. Those of us with a secure attachment style usually find it easier to nurture and sustain close connections, while those with insecure attachment styles (avoidant, anxious, or disorganized) often have trouble in adult relationships. But the good news is that it’s entirely possible to change your patterns. We spoke to Rolnick and three other experts to help us understand the four attachment styles, including how they develop and what you can do to form more secure relationship habits with friends, family, and romantic partners moving forward. Understanding the 4 Attachment Styles Avoidant We might develop an avoidant attachment style if our primary caregiver was emotionally distant or dismissive, per Utah State University . This attachment style can also occur if we were regularly and unreasonably depended on or criticized as a child, Hider Shaaban , a licensed clinical psychologist and founding executive director of Philadelphia Center for Psychotherapy, told Nice News. “So [they] may develop a core belief of ‘If I let people get close to me, they will drain me, judge me, and maybe even hurt me along the way, so it’s safer that I keep my distance.’” Adults with avoidant attachment styles prioritize independence and self-reliance over close connection, added Terri DiMatteo , a licensed professional counselor at Open Door Therapy. “Deep emotional intimacy or vulnerability feels uncomfortable to them,” she said. “When a romantic or non-romantic person gets too close, they are likely to pull away and create distance. Avoidantly attached adults have great difficulty expressing their own emotions, and in the back of their mind is the refrain ‘I don’t need anyone. I am good on my own.’” fizkes—iStock/Getty Images Plus According to the Cleveland Clinic , other potential signs of avoidant attachment include: A strong sense of independence Difficulty trusting people Avoiding physical or emotional intimacy Feeling uncomfortable when people try to get close Being dismissive of others Commitment issues Anxious If you had an inconsistent or emotionally unpredictable caregiver, you might have developed an anxious attachment style, explained Emily Bly , a licensed clinical psychologist and CEO of Psychology Partners Group. When parents “are particularly inconsistent in their emotional responses — vacillating between warm and connected at some moments and cold, nonresponsive, and detached in other moments — [it] can result in the child internalizing a sense that they are ‘not good enough’ or to blame in some way.” Bly added that people with anxious attachment styles tend to fear abandonment and worry that a loved one could withdraw their affection at any time and without warning. They frequently seek reassurance and have trouble believing that people really care for them, and are often on high alert for potential signs of dismissal or rejection. For instance, they might interpret a partner’s subtle shift in tone or a friend’s delayed text response as a signal that something is wrong in the relationship. According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of anxious attachment include: Feeling unworthy of love Difficulty spending time alone High sensitivity to criticism Jealous tendencies Low self-esteem Trouble trusting people Fear of abandonment or rejection Disorganized A disorganized attachment style (also known as fearful avoidant) can occur if a primary caregiver is dangerous or violent. If a parent consistently frightens a child, the child has nowhere to turn in times of distress, Bly explained. As a result, they may develop a “freeze” response to emotional turmoil, feeling that they can’t escape or rely upon their parent. In adulthood, they may shut down and “quasi-dissociate” when stressed, making it difficult for someone else to reach them emotionally, she continued. Relationships can therefore be confusing, as it may feel like the fearful avoidant-attached person has one foot on the gas and another on the brakes. Igor Suka—E+/Getty Images “A person with disorganized attachment craves security and attachment like anyone else, but the fear embedded in this longing will sometimes put the person in a state of ‘system overload,’” Bly said, “where they might be more likely to disappear or ‘ghost’ the attachment figure who tries to get too close to them.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of disorganized attachment include: Difficulty trusting others Trouble with emotional regulation Fear of rejection Confusing, contradictory behaviors Other traits of anxious and avoidant attachments Secure When caregivers provide consistent predictability, abundant love, clear expectations, and straightforward communication, children are often more likely to develop secure attachments. “Basically, they will start to develop the belief system that ‘relationships are generally safe,’ which will help them establish connections with others without the worry of being rejected,” Shaaban said. When they do experience rejection, he added, they’re less likely to take it personally and can bounce back more quickly. People with secure attachment typically view themselves and others positively, communicate honestly and openly, and find it easier to build and maintain lasting, healthy bonds, according to Utah State University. DiMatteo agreed: “Securely attached relationships are safe, relaxed, reliable, and supportive, allowing each person to be their authentic self, knowing they are accepted and valued as they are.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of secure attachment include: Finding it easy to trust others Effective communication Emotional regulation Feeling comfortable spending time alone Finding it easy to connect with others Healthy conflict resolution Being emotionally available to other people How to Become More Secure If you’re prone to forming avoidant, anxious, or disorganized attachments, you can develop an “earned secure” attachment style through healthy adult relationships, positive life experiences, and working with a therapist, per the Cleveland Clinic . Seeing a mental health professional experienced in attachment theory and relationships is especially important if you have a history of trauma, Shaaban noted. You can also try the following to develop healthier, more secure relationship patterns. Understand Your Story: Think about your early childhood and how you developed an insecure attachment style, Bly said. Recognize that your caregiver’s faults, such as inconsistency or emotional distance, reflect their own struggles and have nothing to do with you. With that knowledge, you can begin to rewrite your internal narrative and develop a healthier view of yourself and other people. Seek Out Stable, Secure Relationships: “Be purposeful about seeking out and establishing connections with people who are emotionally mature, consistent, and grounded,” DiMatteo advised. Observing and interacting with securely attached people — including friends, a romantic partner, or a therapist — can help you understand what healthy relationship patterns look like, aiding you in eventually adopting similar behaviors. andreswd—E+/Getty Images Identify Your Triggers: Note the situations that activate your emotional defense mechanisms. “Track your thoughts, bodily sensations, and immediate coping mechanisms when triggered,” Rolnick said. “Writing down your patterns helps you understand yourself rather than running on autopilot.” Practice Honest, Open Communication: Secure attachment involves clear, direct, and authentic interactions with others, and Rolnick suggests working on this by sharing a vulnerable feeling or need with someone you trust once a week. “Vulnerability means something different for every person, and it’s important to gently push your window of tolerance. You might say ‘I felt anxious when I didn’t hear back from you for a few days,’ or ‘I’m having a hard day and feeling anxious — can we talk?’ Each time you face your fear directly, you build your ability to handle similar challenges in the future.” RELATED: Dealing With a Difficult Relationship? Here’s How Psychology Says You Can Shift the Dynamic

items.descriptionOriginal: From a small village in Bihar to screens across India, Purav Jha turned a phone, a passion for acting and a dream into a growing career. Coming from Ranti village, Purav started creating videos with little more than his phone and his ability to make people laugh. But success didn't come overnight. Views were low, recognition was limited, and turning his passion into a career was far from easy. Still, he kept showing up. From playing Poplu to earning recognition as India's “Human AI,” Purav built his identity through performances, comic timing and consistency. Today, his journey from online content creation to acting on OTT platforms reflects years of effort that began far away from the spotlight. His story is a reminder that you don't need an extraordinary beginning to build something meaningful. Sometimes, you just need the courage to keep creating when nobody is watching. Το βακτήριο, το Bacteroides fragilis, παράγει μια τοξίνη που καταστρέφει την προστατευτική επένδυση του παχέος εντέρου, πυροδοτεί χρόνια φλεγμονή και προωθεί το σχηματισμό όγκων.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

items.descriptionOriginal: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton swept floors, bought supplies for children who couldn't afford them, and turned smiles "up instead of down" -- work she once measured against a college degree she never earned and found herself wanting. The custodian who privately carried a sense of failure was, to everyone around her, the living heart of Aubrey Independent School District in Texas. When the superintendent called her to the podium under the pretense of a routine meeting, Hampton unrolled a small red carpet and found her own name printed on it: Marilyn Hampton Elementary School. The next day, she was still crying. "Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them," she said, and in that sentence lives the quiet revelation the story holds: that a life spent in faithful, unglamorous service to others can quietly become the most significant thing in a room, in a district, in a community's memory -- long before anyone thinks to say so out loud.

items.title: Τι κάνει τη Scary Music Scary; Ο συνθέτης "Obsession" για τη δημιουργία μιας ταινίας τρόμου δολοφονίας

Τα βήματά της αντηχούν στη σιωπή προτού εισέλθει ένας δυσοίωνος ήχος, σχεδόν σαν παραμορφωμένος λευκός θόρυβος. Ο…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. Competing Interest Statement: Robinson LS, Darwech I, Knoot CJ, and Harding CM have a financial stake in Omniose, a for-profit entity developing bioconjugate vaccines using patented technology reflected in the data presented in this and other published manuscripts. Source: Washington University in St. Louis The post Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug? appeared first on Futurity .

Karissa: Super spooky and Halloweeny as we prepare for the holiday over the weekend, and a time change over in the US. I know over in Amsterdam, you’re already having those darker evenings. Arielle: Yes, we had our time change last weekend, and yeah, it does get dark so early, and it feels quite wintry, but that’s all right. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I miss the sun. I know. I can’t wait to dive into them. But before we do- Mm … that, we wanna remind you that all these solutions are available in our newsletter format, whether you want that every day or just a weekly digest. It’s free to sign up, and the link to do that is in the show notes. Arielle: If you’re more of a social media feed type of news consumer, then you can follow us on all social platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are, @OdeToOptimism. With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak.
